title: Qupertino: Pure MLX Array Kernels versus Hand-Tuned Metal Shaders for Quantum Circuit Simulation on Apple Silicon
summary: We present Qupertino, an open-source quantum circuit simulator for Apple Silicon, and use it to ask how far a simulator written purely in MLX array operations can go and what remains for hand-tuned Metal shaders. The framework ships two measured tiers. The pure tier dispatches structured gates to specialized MLX kernels: diagonal gates run as broadcast phase multiplies, controlled gates as masked half-state updates, and SWAP as an axis permutation; a paired dense-path ablation attributes a 25-33x speedup to this dispatch alone. The opt-in shader tier adds hand-written Metal kernels for every structured layer family in our benchmarks, including phase-LUT diagonals, GF(2) affine permutation gathers, fused tensor-product single-qubit layers, radix-4 QFT and Walsh-Hadamard butterflies, and basis-conjugated XX/YY Trotter layers; runtime fusion detectors route work to them while preserving circuit semantics exactly, confirmed by parity tests. In a four-way interleaved campaign on M1 Max (two warmups, ten measured repeats per cell), the shader tier is fastest by mean runtime in all 18 comparison cells against same-machine Qiskit Aer CPU and PennyLane lightning.qubit. At 25 qubits, gate-stream QFT runs in 0.0591 +/- 0.0029 s (paired 47.2x over Aer, 95.3x over PennyLane) and TFIM Trotter evolution in 0.495 +/- 0.035 s (36.2x and 67.2x). Across a 29-workload suite, the shader tier's paired speedup over pure MLX reaches 25x, with 25 of 29 workloads accelerating above parity. The framework also supports variational ansatz workloads, QAOA, QCBM, Trotter-Suzuki Hamiltonian simulation, and OpenQASM 2.0 import (unitary subset); a preliminary MPS backend reaches 150 qubits on limited-entanglement workloads. Correctness rests on 253 Python tests, independent complex128 checks, and a Trotter-error curve against exact diagonalization. State-vector memory remains exponential in qubit count.

AI.tldr: Qupertino is an open-source quantum circuit simulator for Apple Silicon built on MLX, with a pure MLX tier and an optional hand-written Metal shader tier. It achieves large speedups over CPU-based Qiskit Aer and PennyLane lightning.qubit across 18 benchmark cells and a 29-workload suite.
AI.motivation: To explore how far a quantum circuit simulator written purely in MLX array operations can go on Apple Silicon, and what performance gains still require hand-tuned Metal shaders.
AI.method: Two-tier design: (1) a pure tier dispatching structured gates to specialized MLX kernels (diagonal gates as broadcast phase multiplies, controlled gates as masked half-state updates, SWAP as axis permutation); (2) an opt-in shader tier with hand-written Metal kernels for structured layer families (phase-LUT diagonals, GF(2) affine permutation gathers, fused tensor-product single-qubit layers, radix-4 QFT/Walsh-Hadamard butterflies, basis-conjugated XX/YY Trotter layers), routed by runtime fusion detectors that preserve circuit semantics.
AI.result: On M1 Max across a four-way interleaved campaign, the shader tier is fastest by mean runtime in all 18 comparison cells against same-machine Qiskit Aer CPU and PennyLane lightning.qubit. At 25 qubits, gate-stream QFT runs in 0.0591 +/- 0.0029 s (47.2x over Aer, 95.3x over PennyLane) and TFIM Trotter evolution in 0.495 +/- 0.035 s (36.2x and 67.2x). Across 29 workloads, the shader tier reaches up to 25x paired speedup over pure MLX, with 25 of 29 above parity. It supports variational ansatze, QAOA, QCBM, Trotter-Suzuki simulation, and OpenQASM 2.0 import; a preliminary MPS backend reaches 150 qubits on limited-entanglement workloads. Correctness is validated by 253 Python tests, independent complex128 checks, and a Trotter-error curve against exact diagonalization.
AI.conclusion: Qupertino demonstrates that a pure MLX simulator achieves strong performance on Apple Silicon, while hand-tuned Metal shaders provide further substantial gains (up to 25x over the pure tier) and consistent superiority over CPU baselines. State-vector memory remains exponential in qubit count, motivating the MPS backend.

title: AlchemQ: Proof-Carrying Quantum Circuit Optimization with Per-Result Equivalence Certificates
comment: 25 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables. Pilot run on IBM Heron r2. Certificate spec, reference verifier, benchmark and certificate corpora, raw hardware data: https://github.com/a1damek1125/AlchemQ (code Apache-2.0, data CC BY 4.0), archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.XXXXXXXX . Engine proprietary; certificates verifiable without it. LLM-assisted drafting; see Acknowledgments
summary: We present AlchemQ v0.5, a proof-of-concept system that couples an untrusted beam-search optimizer with a machine-checkable per-result certification layer and a versioned certificate protocol (0.2.0), so that every optimized circuit ships with a verifiable artifact rather than a bare claim. The certifier proves equivalence up to global phase by ZX-calculus full reduction, with a numeric-tensor fallback based on the optimal Hilbert-Schmidt overlap. Certificates are self-contained and tamper-evident: canonical gate-canon-v1 hashes, measured residuals, tri-state verdicts (certified/rejected/inconclusive), and versioned phase-note schemas for cross-platform reproducibility. The agent aggregates three fuzzy t-norms, cannot return an uncertified circuit, and since v0.4 guarantees no componentwise regression against the original. On a benchmark of 100 circuits, all 400 optimizations terminate without error, every returned circuit is certified, every mutation is detected, and a 2998-test suite passes on two platforms. The PyZX baseline is strong (21.4% mean T-count reduction over 82 circuits) and the agent is strictly better on 9/100; the three t-norms return identical circuits on all 100 standard instances, diverging only on 4/38 of an adversarial suite. Two case studies are new: a false negative root-caused to a pivot-normalization bug in PyZX's compare_tensors (pivot 4.7e-9; the optimal-overlap residual is 7.4e-11), and eight certificates rejected on macOS due to BLAS-dependent floats in phase_note. Both were fixed; all artifact sets validate 400/400 on both platforms. A pilot run on IBM Heron r2 gives a certified circuit 78% shallower with 65% fewer two-qubit gates; output quality favors it on all three metrics but is not significant at 1024 shots. We release the certificate specification and a standalone reference verifier (Apache-2.0) with data and scripts; the engine is proprietary.

title: Femtoscopic Correlation Functions in Density Operator Representation
summary: Femtoscopic correlation functions (CFs) have been increasingly used to extract strong interactions between pairs of unstable particles, but their physical soundness has recently been questioned. To answer this, we formulate CFs at the operator level, with the observed subsystem described by a reduced density operator and subsequent dynamics absorbed into an effective measurement operator. The Koonin-Pratt form is recovered under four well-motivated reductions. The formulation makes explicit that the source-side and interaction-side representations must be consistently matched, and motivates an operational convention in which a measured reference correlation establishes a compatible source--interaction pairing that can be extended to other pairs for CF-to-CF predictions.

AI.tldr: This paper puts femtoscopic correlation functions on a rigorous operator-level footing, showing the Koonin–Pratt form emerges only under four explicit reductions and requiring consistent source–interaction matching.
AI.motivation: Femtoscopic correlation functions are now widely used to extract strong interactions between unstable particle pairs, yet their physical soundness has recently been questioned. A rigorous foundation is needed to clarify when and why CF extraction is valid.
AI.method: The authors formulate CFs at the operator level: the observed subsystem is described by a reduced density operator, with subsequent dynamics absorbed into an effective measurement operator. The Koonin–Pratt form is then recovered under four well-motivated reductions.
AI.result: The operator formulation shows explicitly that the source-side and interaction-side representations must be consistently matched, and it recovers the Koonin–Pratt form only under four specific reductions.
AI.conclusion: The work motivates an operational convention in which a measured reference correlation establishes a compatible source–interaction pairing that can be extended to other pairs, enabling CF-to-CF predictions.

title: Reconfigurable Current Distributions in Percolating Au Films and CrO2 Powder Compacts - Beyond Geometrical Connectivity
summary: Despite fundamental differences in morphology, dimensionality, and microscopic transport, semicontinuous Au films and compacted CrO2 powders converge on a common network-level principle: the electrically relevant network is a condition-dependent subset of the physical contact network. In Au films near the geometrical percolation threshold, increasing bias reversibly shifts the low-temperature response from activated nearest-neighbour hopping with negative magnetoresistance to a weak-localization-like regime with positive magnetoresistance, consistent with broader electronic participation of the fixed island network. In CrO2 powder compacts, magnetic field mainly changes the spin-dependent resistances of existing intergranular junctions and thereby reorders competing current paths; temperature and measuring current can additionally expand or deplete the active network. Cohn's theorem provides a compact sensitivity principle for both cases: local resistance changes influence the measured response in proportion to the current carried by the affected links. The comparison identifies two limiting but interconvertible modes of reconfiguration - link enabling and link reweighting - and shows why geometrical connectivity alone is insufficient for interpreting transport in strongly inhomogeneous conductors.

AI.tldr: Semicontinuous Au films and compacted CrO2 powders share a network-level principle: the electrically relevant network is a condition-dependent subset of the physical contact network. Au films exhibit bias-tunable crossover from activated nearest-neighbour hopping (negative MR) to a weak-localization-like regime (positive MR); CrO2 compacts show field-driven reordering of spin-dependent junction resistances. Two interconvertible reconfiguration modes—link enabling and link reweighting—are identified.
AI.motivation: To reconcile transport in two morphologically, dimensionally, and microscopically distinct systems (semicontinuous Au films and compacted CrO2 powders) and to test whether geometrical connectivity alone suffices to interpret transport in strongly inhomogeneous conductors.
AI.method: Comparative network-level analysis of magnetotransport in semicontinuous Au films near the geometrical percolation threshold (variable-bias measurements) and in CrO2 powder compacts (magnetic field, temperature, and measuring-current variation), interpreted via Cohn's theorem relating local resistance changes to measured response through the current carried by the affected links.
AI.result: In Au films, increasing bias reversibly shifts the low-temperature response from activated nearest-neighbour hopping with negative magnetoresistance to a weak-localization-like regime with positive magnetoresistance, consistent with broader electronic participation of the fixed island network. In CrO2 compacts, magnetic field mainly alters spin-dependent resistances of existing intergranular junctions, reordering competing current paths, while temperature and measuring current expand or deplete the active network.

title: Holomorphic Quantum Error Correction Codes
summary: We develop a holomorphic representation of quantum error correction codes (QECCs) within the Segal--Bargmann space. By encoding qubits into Schwinger boson modes $(z_{a_j}, z_{b_j})$ subject to a degree-one homogeneity constraint, we derive closed-form differential operator representations for stabilizers, syndrome extraction, and recovery for fundamental codes (three-, five-, seven-, and nine-qubit codes). Quantum errors are characterized as holomorphic perturbations violating this constraint, while syndrome measurement projects onto eigenspaces of commuting differential operators. Restricting to unit-magnitude variables ($|z|=1$) reveals a toroidal space $\T^{2n}$ where error syndromes manifest as discrete translations in winding number space $\Z^{2n}$, and recovery acts as Hamiltonian flows restoring the winding configuration. In the full Segal--Bargmann space, the code space is a holomorphic submanifold of $\CP^{2^n-1}$, with correctable errors as transverse normal directions. Consequently, the Knill--Laflamme condition becomes a Fubini--Study orthogonality condition between the code submanifold and its error-translated images. Topological protection emerges from the $U(1)^n$ fiber bundle structure: global phase noise along fibers is unobservable, while base-space errors require active correction. Finally, we establish a path-integral formulation for semiclassical error correction dynamics and show that geometric entanglement via the Segre embedding naturally quantifies code distance. This framework unifies algebraic, geometric, and topological perspectives on fault-tolerant quantum protocols.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a holomorphic representation of quantum error correction codes (QECCs) in the Segal–Bargmann space, reformulating stabilizers, syndrome extraction, and recovery as differential operators, and recasting code conditions, topological protection, and code distance in geometric and topological terms.
AI.motivation: Quantum error correction is typically described algebraically, but a unified geometric and topological perspective linking stabilizer codes, the Knill–Laflamme condition, and fault tolerance is lacking. The authors aim to provide such a unifying framework via the Segal–Bargmann (holomorphic) representation.
AI.method: Qubits are encoded into Schwinger boson modes (z_{a_j}, z_{b_j}) with a degree-one homogeneity constraint, yielding closed-form differential operator representations of stabilizers, syndrome extraction, and recovery for the three-, five-, seven-, and nine-qubit codes. Errors become holomorphic perturbations violating the constraint; syndrome measurement projects onto eigenspaces of commuting differential operators. Restricting to |z|=1 gives a toroidal space T^{2n} where syndromes act as discrete winding-number translations Z^{2n} and recovery as Hamiltonian flows. In the full space, the code space is a holomorphic submanifold of CP^{2^n−1} with correctable errors as transverse normal directions, so the Knill–Laflamme condition becomes a Fubini–Study orthogonality condition. A path-integral formulation is established for semiclassical dynamics, and geometric entanglement via the Segre embedding quantifies code distance.
AI.result: Closed-form differential operator representations are obtained for stabilizers, syndrome extraction, and recovery of fundamental codes; error syndromes appear as discrete translations in winding-number space; the Knill–Laflamme condition is recast as Fubini–Study orthogonality; topological protection emerges from a U(1)^n fiber bundle structure (global phase noise along fibers is unobservable, base-space errors require active correction); and geometric entanglement via the Segre embedding naturally quantifies code distance.
AI.conclusion: The Segal–Bargmann holomorphic framework unifies algebraic, geometric, and topological perspectives on fault-tolerant quantum protocols, providing a coherent description of QECCs in which syndromes, recovery, protection, and code distance all acquire geometric/topological meaning.

title: TetrisCNN for interpretable detection of phases of matter from experimental quantum simulator data
summary: Detecting phases of matter in general relies on identifying the correct order parameter - a task that remains notoriously difficult for unknown transitions and traditionally is guided by physical intuition and educated guess. Neural networks have recently offered an alternative route by locating phase transitions in known models without any a priori physical knowledge. Yet these approaches remain black boxes and only identify phases without elucidating their properties. Moreover, they often struggle when confronted with realistic, noisy experimental data, which constitute the ultimate testbed for automated methods in physics. Here, we bridge these perspectives by introducing TetrisCNN, a convolutional architecture with parallel branches of differently shaped filters, reminiscent of Tetris blocks, that learns sparse, interpretable latent representations directly in terms of spin correlators. Applied to experimental snapshots of two-dimensional Ising and XY quantum simulators measured in multiple bases, the network not only detects phase transitions and crossovers but also expresses its latent representation and decision boundaries as symbolic formulas built from experimentally measurable spin correlators. This framework opens the way to integrating interpretable neural networks with quantum simulators to uncover and understand new phases of matter.

AI.tldr: TetrisCNN is a branched convolutional architecture that learns sparse, interpretable latent representations in terms of spin correlators, enabling phase detection and symbolic order-parameter discovery directly from noisy experimental quantum simulator data.
AI.motivation: Identifying the correct order parameter for phase transitions is notoriously difficult and traditionally relies on physical intuition, especially for unknown transitions. Prior neural-network approaches detect phase transitions without a priori knowledge but remain black boxes (identifying phases without explaining their properties) and often fail on realistic, noisy experimental data.
AI.method: TetrisCNN: a convolutional architecture with parallel branches of differently shaped filters, reminiscent of Tetris blocks, that learns sparse, interpretable latent representations directly in terms of spin correlators. Applied to experimental snapshots of 2D Ising and XY quantum simulators measured in multiple bases.
AI.result: The network detects phase transitions and crossovers, and expresses its latent representation and decision boundaries as symbolic formulas built from experimentally measurable spin correlators, all on noisy experimental data.
AI.conclusion: The framework opens the way to integrating interpretable neural networks with quantum simulators to uncover and understand new phases of matter.

title: Energy-Constrained Commutator Variance for Weyl Pairs
summary: Let $W$ be a representation of the Weyl relations on a separable Hilbert space and write $\mathcal R_W(K)=\{W(f):f\in K\}''$. If the symplectic pairing of $K_1$ and $K_2$ is nonzero, there is a self-adjoint unitary $B\in\mathcal R_W(K_2)$ such that, for every normal state $ρ$, one can choose a self-adjoint unitary $A_ρ\in\mathcal R_W(K_1)$ with $\operatorname{Var}_ρ(-i[A_ρ,B])=4$. Hence the optimized mean-input-energy-constrained coefficient equals $4$ at every admissible energy threshold. For the fixed trigonometric Weyl witness $h$, an exact identity for $4-h^2$ reduces the deficit to a phase-fixed problem for commuting squared Weyl translations. For the one-mode quadratic energy $G_M=\frac12 R^TMR-\frac12\sqrt{\det M}$, with $M>0$ and $u^TΩv=π$, we prove $4-γ_{G_M,E}(h)=\frac{u^TMu+v^TMv+2π\sqrt{\det M}}{4E}+O(E^{-2})$. The lower bound holds over all normal states satisfying the mean-energy constraint, and a localized Zak construction attains the same coefficient. For $G=dΓ(H_1)$ and witness directions $u,v\in\operatorname{dom}H_1^{1/2}$, the fixed-witness deficit is $Θ(E^{-1})$ whenever at least one direction lies outside $\ker H_1$; if both directions are zero modes, the constrained supremum equals the endpoint at every positive threshold.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes that for two Weyl subsystems with nonzero symplectic pairing, an optimized mean-input-energy-constrained Bell/Weyl coefficient equals exactly 4 at every admissible energy threshold, with refined asymptotics for the deficit $4-\gamma_{G,E}(h)$ given by a phase-fixed commuting-translation problem leading to explicit $O(E^{-1})$ and $O(E^{-2})$ expansions.
AI.motivation: The work is motivated by quantifying quantum nonlocal correlations (Bell-type/Weyl coefficients) under physical constraints, specifically a mean-input-energy constraint. The goal is to determine the exact optimal coefficient and characterize how the deficit from its maximal value behaves as the energy threshold grows.
AI.method: The authors use the representation theory of the Weyl relations on a separable Hilbert space, studying von Neumann algebras $\mathcal R_W(K)=\{W(f):f\in K\}''$. They construct self-adjoint unitaries $B\in\mathcal R_W(K_2)$ and $A_\rho\in\mathcal R_W(K_1)$ achieving variance $\operatorname{Var}_\rho(-i[A_\rho,B])=4$, and reduce the deficit $4-h^2$ to a phase-fixed problem for commuting squared Weyl translations using an exact identity. For the one-mode quadratic energy $G_M$ they analytically derive asymptotic expansions, and they employ a localized Zak construction to attain the lower bound. Additionally, they analyze $G=d\Gamma(H_1)$ with witness directions in $\operatorname{dom}H_1^{1/2}$.
AI.result: If the symplectic pairing of $K_1$ and $K_2$ is nonzero, there exists $B\in\mathcal R_W(K_2)$ such that for every normal state $\rho$ one can pick $A_\rho\in\mathcal R_W(K_1)$ with $\operatorname{Var}_\rho(-i[A_\rho,B])=4$, so the optimized mean-input-energy-constrained coefficient equals $4$ at every admissible energy threshold. For the fixed trigonometric Weyl witness $h$, an exact identity for $4-h^2$ yields a phase-fixed problem. For the one-mode quadratic energy $G_M=\frac12 R^TMR-\frac12\sqrt{\det M}$ with $M>0$, $u^T\Omega v=\pi$, they prove $4-\gamma_{G_M,E}(h)=\frac{u^TMu+v^TMv+2\pi\sqrt{\det M}}{4E}+O(E^{-2})$, with the lower bound valid over all mean-energy-constrained normal states and attained by a localized Zak construction. For $G=d\Gamma(H_1)$ and witness directions $u,v\in\operatorname{dom}H_1^{1/2}$, the fixed-witness deficit is $\Theta(E^{-1})$ whenever at least one direction lies outside $\ker H_1$; if both are zero modes, the constrained supremum equals the endpoint at every positive threshold.
AI.conclusion: The optimized energy-constrained Weyl/Bell coefficient saturates at 4 under nonzero symplectic pairing regardless of the energy threshold, and the deficit from the fixed-witness maximum admits sharp asymptotic characterizations: an explicit $O(E^{-1})$ leading term with $O(E^{-2})$ correction for one-mode quadratic energies, and a $\Theta(E^{-1})$ rate for $d\Gamma(H_1)$ except in the degenerate two-zero-mode case where the constrained supremum already reaches the endpoint.

title: Suzuki-Trotter Decompositions and other Methods for Quantum Time Evolution
comment: 32 + 10 pages, 6 figures, 4 tables; topical review, comments welcome!
summary: (Suzuki-)Trotter decompositions, splitting methods, (Lie) product formulae... The most common numerical methods for the time evolution of quantum systems come with many names. And they are used practically everywhere with applications ranging from the solution of classical equations of motion and various Monte Carlo simulations to the real and imaginary time evolution on classical as well as quantum computers. Here we review the state of the art of said methods, focussing especially on the progress made over the last few years. We highlight recently discovered efficient time evolution algorithms and explain how best to use them in practice. A central part of this work is the estimation of error bounds that has improved greatly within the past decade. The relevance of time evolution methods for quantum computing is discussed with a focus on noisy hardware. Finally, a comprehensive overview of generalisations, related methods and alternatives to Trotterization is provided. This includes time-dependent Hamiltonian dynamics, processed methods, multi-product formulae, symplectic integrators, TDVP for tensor networks, quantum signal processing, Crouch-Grossman methods and more. The overall perspective in this work is that of a theoretical physicist. All mathematical proofs as well as some technical details are omitted for easier readability. Instead, this review serves as a hands-on guide and, of course, as a starting point for references that provide further details.

AI.tldr: A hands-on review of the state of the art in (Suzuki-)Trotter decompositions, splitting methods and product formulae for time evolution of quantum systems, emphasizing recent algorithmic advances, greatly improved error bounds, noisy-hardware quantum computing relevance, and a broad survey of generalizations and alternatives.
AI.motivation: These decomposition/splitting methods are ubiquitous for simulating time evolution across classical equations of motion, Monte Carlo simulations, and real/imaginary time evolution on classical and quantum computers. However, the field has advanced rapidly in recent years (new efficient algorithms, much better error bounds), and a unified, practically oriented overview was lacking.
AI.method: A review written from a theoretical physicist's perspective. It surveys state-of-the-art (Suzuki-)Trotter decompositions, splitting methods, and (Lie) product formulae, focusing on progress of the last few years. It highlights recently discovered efficient time evolution algorithms and explains their best practical use, with a central emphasis on estimating error bounds. Mathematical proofs and technical details are omitted for readability.
AI.result: The review consolidates recent progress: improved error-bound estimation over the past decade, new efficient time evolution algorithms with practical usage guidance, and a discussion of the relevance of time evolution methods for quantum computing with a focus on noisy hardware.
AI.conclusion: Serves as a hands-on guide and a starting point for further references, providing a comprehensive overview of generalizations, related methods, and alternatives to Trotterization, including time-dependent Hamiltonian dynamics, processed methods, multi-product formulae, symplectic integrators, TDVP for tensor networks, quantum signal processing, and Crouch-Grossman methods.

title: Enhanced Emission and Two-Photon Interference of Lead-Vacancy Centers in Diamond Solid Immersion Lenses
summary: A negatively charged lead-vacancy (PbV-) center in diamond is a novel quantum system which can be operated at a high temperature above 4 K owing to its large ground state splitting. To unlock the quantum properties of the PbV- center, the enhancement of the fluorescence intensity is a key issue. Here, we demonstrate enhanced emission from PbV- centers by a factor of approximately 10 using solid immersion lenses (SILs) fabricated on rough diamond surface caused by high-temperature anneal over 2000°C. Resonant excitation reveals the narrow emission close to the transform-limited linewidth. Furthermore, we demonstrate two-photon interference using one single PbV- center in an SIL. This enhanced emission and indistinguishability will lead to further development of the PbV- center towards quantum network node applications.

AI.tldr: Fabricating solid immersion lenses on rough diamond surfaces enhances PbV- center emission by ~10x, enabling near transform-limited lines and two-photon interference.
AI.motivation: The negatively charged lead-vacancy center (PbV-) in diamond is a promising quantum system operable above 4 K due to its large ground-state splitting. However, unlocking its quantum properties is limited by weak fluorescence intensity, so emission enhancement is a key issue.
AI.method: The authors fabricated solid immersion lenses (SILs) on rough diamond surfaces produced by high-temperature annealing above 2000°C, and used resonant excitation to characterize the emission. They also performed two-photon interference measurements using a single PbV- center in an SIL.
AI.result: Emission from PbV- centers was enhanced by approximately 10x. Resonant excitation revealed narrow emission close to the transform-limited linewidth, and two-photon interference was demonstrated with a single PbV- center in an SIL.
AI.conclusion: The combination of enhanced emission and photon indistinguishability advances PbV- centers toward quantum network node applications.

title: Lazy training of quantum physics informed neural networks
summary: We study the gradient-flow training dynamics of quantum physics-informed neural networks (QPINNs) for the solution of second-order elliptic partial differential equations with Dirichlet boundary conditions. We consider parameterized quantum circuits as function approximators and analyze their overparameterized regime through the lens of the neural tangent kernel (NTK). Our contribution is a nonasymptotic lazy-training theory for QPINNs and their variational formulation: we prove that, for sufficiently large circuit width, the nonlinear gradient flow is quantitatively approximated by a linearized NTK model, with explicit bounds depending on the number of qubits, circuit depth, circuit light-cone geometry, and the dimension of the domain of the solution to the PDE.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a nonasymptotic lazy-training theory for quantum physics-informed neural networks (QPINNs) solving second-order elliptic PDEs with Dirichlet boundary conditions, proving that for sufficiently large circuit width the nonlinear gradient flow is quantitatively approximated by a linearized NTK model.
AI.motivation: QPINNs combine parameterized quantum circuits with physics-informed training to solve PDEs, but their training dynamics—particularly in the overparameterized regime—lack theoretical guarantees. A rigorous understanding of when and how gradient flow training behaves predictably is needed.
AI.method: The authors treat parameterized quantum circuits as function approximators for second-order elliptic PDEs with Dirichlet boundary conditions, and analyze their overparameterized regime through the neural tangent kernel (NTK) lens. They establish a nonasymptotic result showing that, for sufficiently large circuit width, the nonlinear gradient flow is quantitatively approximated by a linearized NTK model, with explicit bounds.
AI.result: A nonasymptotic lazy-training theory for QPINNs and their variational formulation is proven, with explicit error bounds that depend on the number of qubits, circuit depth, circuit light-cone geometry, and the dimension of the PDE solution domain.
AI.conclusion: QPINNs in the large-width regime admit a quantitative linearized NTK description, providing theoretical grounding for their gradient-flow training dynamics that scales explicitly with circuit and problem parameters.

title: Achieving the limits of automorphism gates
comment: 15 pages in the main text (5 figures, 1 table); 104 pages total (5 figures, 10 tables)
summary: Universal fault-tolerant quantum computing combines versatile but expensive operations with specialized but cheap ones. Its efficiency depends on how much computation can be pushed onto the cheap operations and on the size of the code needed to do so. Automorphism gates provide such cheap operations using only physical single-qubit Clifford gates and qubit permutations. Yet no general theory characterizes their maximum logical power or the minimum code size needed to attain it. We develop such a theory. For stabilizer codes encoding $k\geq3$ logical qubits, we show that the largest logical group attainable by automorphisms is generated by all addressable $S$ and $\mathrm{CX}$ gates, and we construct codes attaining it. While this group contains exponentially fewer gates than the full Clifford group, adding one suitable non-Clifford gate yields universality. We further classify the largest logical groups attainable using qubit permutations, physical single-qubit Cliffords, or both across general stabilizer and CSS codes, and derive refined bounds for self-dual CSS subclasses. Achieving the maximum-size logical group through automorphisms requires $n=Θ(2^k)$ physical qubits. By contrast, all addressable diagonal Clifford gates, generated by $S$ and $\mathrm{CZ}$, require only $n=Θ(k^2)$ physical qubits when implemented using physical single-qubit Cliffords alone. Both bounds are tight. This polynomial qubit cost extends beyond Cliffords to all addressable diagonal gates at any fixed level of the Clifford hierarchy, using physical single-qubit diagonal gates. Thus, for full addressability, the sharpest physical-qubit cost divide lies between diagonal and $\mathrm{CX}$-type gates, not between Clifford and non-Clifford gates.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a general theory of automorphism gates in stabilizer codes, characterizing the maximum logical groups attainable and deriving tight physical-qubit cost bounds that reveal a sharp divide between diagonal and CX-type gates.
AI.motivation: Universal fault-tolerant quantum computing benefits from pushing computation onto cheap operations like automorphism gates (physical single-qubit Cliffords plus qubit permutations). However, no general theory existed to characterize their maximum logical power or the minimum code size needed to achieve it.
AI.method: The authors analyze stabilizer codes (including CSS and self-dual CSS subclasses) and classify the largest logical groups attainable using automorphisms, qubit permutations, physical single-qubit Cliffords, or combinations thereof. They construct codes attaining these maximal groups and derive tight bounds on the required number of physical qubits.
AI.result: For stabilizer codes with k ≥ 3 logical qubits, the largest automorphism-attainable logical group is generated by all addressable S and CX gates, requiring n = Θ(2^k) physical qubits. Adding one suitable non-Clifford gate yields universality. In contrast, addressable diagonal Cliffords (S and CZ) need only n = Θ(k^2) qubits. This polynomial cost extends to all addressable diagonal gates at any fixed Clifford-hierarchy level.
AI.conclusion: For full addressability, the sharpest physical-qubit cost divide lies between diagonal and CX-type gates, not between Clifford and non-Clifford gates.

title: Theory of post-selected entanglement transitions in monitored bosons
summary: Entanglement phase transitions driven by quantum measurements have emerged as a central paradigm in open quantum many-body physics. Such phase transitions are well established for systems with finite local Hilbert-space dimensions, such as qubits and fermions, while their realization in bosonic systems with unbounded local occupation numbers remains poorly understood. Even in the absence of interactions, number states of bosons are intrinsically non-Gaussian, preventing the use of standard correlation-matrix approaches. To address this problem, we develop a replica-free Keldysh field-theoretic framework that expresses the Renyi entropy of bosonic systems initialized in on-site Fock states in terms of permanents of matrices constructed from single-particle Green's functions. Applying this framework to a continuously monitored one-dimensional cross-stitch lattice conditioned on the no-click trajectory, we uncover a transition from volume-law to logarithmic entanglement scaling. We show that the transition is controlled by a restructuring of the non-Hermitian spectrum that changes the number of long-lived modes from extensive to finite. In the strongly monitored regime, bosons dynamically condense into a microscopic number of slowest-decaying modes, producing logarithmic entanglement scaling, whereas an extensive manifold of long-lived modes at weak monitoring gives rise to volume-law entanglement. Our results establish a distinct mechanism for measurement-induced entanglement transitions in free bosonic systems and provide a computationally efficient diagnostic of the measurement-induced bosonic condensation.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a replica-free Keldysh field-theoretic framework for bosonic measurement-induced entanglement transitions, expressing Renyi entropy of on-site Fock states via permanents of Green's-function matrices, and reveals a volume-law to logarithmic transition in a monitored 1D cross-stitch lattice driven by non-Hermitian spectral restructuring.
AI.motivation: Measurement-induced entanglement phase transitions are well established for finite local Hilbert-space dimensions (qubits, fermions), but their realization in bosonic systems with unbounded occupation numbers is poorly understood even without interactions, since number states are intrinsically non-Gaussian and standard correlation-matrix methods fail.
AI.method: A replica-free Keldysh field-theoretic framework that expresses the Renyi entropy of bosonic systems initialized in on-site Fock states as permanents of matrices built from single-particle Green's functions. This is applied to a continuously monitored one-dimensional cross-stitch lattice conditioned on the no-click trajectory.
AI.result: A transition from volume-law to logarithmic entanglement scaling is uncovered. The transition is controlled by a restructuring of the non-Hermitian spectrum that changes the number of long-lived modes from extensive to finite: strong monitoring yields dynamical condensation into a microscopic number of slowest-decaying modes with logarithmic scaling, while weak monitoring gives an extensive manifold of long-lived modes and volume-law entanglement.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a distinct mechanism for measurement-induced entanglement transitions in free bosonic systems and provide a computationally efficient diagnostic of measurement-induced bosonic condensation.

title: Emergent classicality and wavefunction branching in an isolated quantum many-body system
summary: Decoherence in quantum systems is conventionally modeled as the effect of interactions with an external environment. However, such a prescription excludes isolated many-body systems, which are also expected to display classical behavior at macroscopic scales. In isolated systems, decoherence must emerge internally from microscopic degrees of freedom that are invisible to the macroscopic description. Here we explicitly show that classicality can emerge in such a fashion. We consider a weakly disordered, $3$-local chaotic kicked top of $N$ qubits, where the collective spin sector serves as the macroscopic description, while the microscopic permutation sector acts as an internal bath, decohering the collective spin sector. Starting from closed unitary dynamics, we derive and numerically confirm an effective Lindblad equation for the collective spin variables. In the thermodynamic limit these reduced dynamics converge to a classical chaotic Fokker--Planck equation with vanishingly small diffusion on the spherical phase space, producing a quantum-classical correspondence beyond the Ehrenfest time. The chaotic dynamics evolve the pure many-body wavefunction into continuously branching components associated with distinct classical trajectories. These branches acquire nearly orthogonal microscopic records in the permutation sector, preventing quantum interferences and ensuring the corresponding histories remain consistent.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that classicality emerges internally in isolated many-body systems: using a weakly disordered 3-local chaotic kicked top of N qubits, the permutation sector acts as an internal bath that decoheres the collective spin sector, yielding an effective Lindblad equation and, in the thermodynamic limit, a classical chaotic Fokker–Planck equation.
AI.motivation: Decoherence is conventionally attributed to external environments, a prescription that cannot account for isolated many-body systems, which are nonetheless expected to exhibit classical behavior at macroscopic scales. In isolated systems, decoherence must arise internally from microscopic degrees of freedom invisible to the macroscopic description, and the paper aims to show explicitly that classicality can emerge in this manner.
AI.method: The authors study a weakly disordered, 3-local chaotic kicked top of N qubits, treating the collective spin sector as the macroscopic description and the microscopic permutation sector as an internal bath. Starting from closed unitary dynamics, they derive an effective Lindblad equation for the collective spin variables and numerically confirm it.
AI.result: In the thermodynamic limit the reduced dynamics converge to a classical chaotic Fokker–Planck equation with vanishingly small diffusion on the spherical phase space, producing a quantum-classical correspondence beyond the Ehrenfest time. The chaotic dynamics evolve the pure many-body wavefunction into continuously branching components tied to distinct classical trajectories, which acquire nearly orthogonal microscopic records in the permutation sector.
AI.conclusion: Internal decoherence from microscopic permutation-sector degrees of freedom suffices to generate classicality in isolated many-body systems. The nearly orthogonal records prevent quantum interferences and ensure the corresponding histories remain consistent, establishing an emergent quantum-to-classical transition without an external environment.

title: A Square-Root Barrier to Quantum Gate Speed under Linear Coupling
summary: Faster quantum gates can suppress the decoherence accumulated during a computation, but in superconducting processors stronger microwave pulses can also increase leakage, off-resonant excitation, stray-field errors, and crosstalk. This creates a central energy--speed--error tradeoff: can quantum state engineering make a gate parametrically faster without paying proportionally more drive energy? We address this question by treating the driving pulse as a quantum bosonic field rather than a classical waveform. For a finite-dimensional system coupled linearly to that field, we prove that fixed-fidelity gate transition rates grow at most as the square root of the pulse energy, under stated uniformity conditions on the coupling and accepted dynamics. The bound permits arbitrary pulse states, including squeezed and non-Gaussian states, as well as drive--system entanglement and back action; coherent Gaussian pulses attain its energy exponent. Thus squeezing or other state engineering alone cannot replace the square-root energy law of a conventional linear drive by the linear scaling allowed by general quantum speed limits. Achieving that improvement requires changing the interaction class, in addition to using a suitable nonclassical pulse, thereby identifying interaction nonlinearity as an essential resource for relaxing the practical gate-speed error tradeoff.

AI.tldr: Treating the drive as a quantum bosonic field, the authors prove that fixed-fidelity gate transition rates grow at most as the square root of pulse energy, so state engineering alone cannot beat the conventional linear-drive energy scaling; nonlinear interaction is required.
AI.motivation: Faster superconducting quantum gates suppress decoherence but stronger microwave pulses raise leakage, off-resonant excitation, stray-field errors, and crosstalk, creating an energy–speed–error tradeoff. The key question is whether quantum state engineering can make a gate parametrically faster without proportionally more drive energy, i.e., whether the linear (square-root energy) scaling of a conventional drive can be improved.
AI.method: The driving pulse is modeled as a quantum bosonic field rather than a classical waveform, with a finite-dimensional system coupled linearly to that field. Under stated uniformity conditions on the coupling and accepted dynamics, a bound on fixed-fidelity gate transition rates is derived that holds for arbitrary pulse states (including squeezed and non-Gaussian states), drive–system entanglement, and back action.
AI.result: Fixed-fidelity gate transition rates grow at most as the square root of the pulse energy. Coherent Gaussian pulses attain exactly this energy exponent, while general quantum speed limits would permit linear scaling. No pulse state engineering, including squeezing or non-Gaussian states, exceeds the square-root law.
AI.conclusion: Squeezing or other state engineering alone cannot replace the square-root energy law of a conventional linear drive with the linear scaling allowed by general quantum speed limits. Relaxing the practical gate-speed–error tradeoff requires changing the interaction class in addition to using a suitable nonclassical pulse, identifying interaction nonlinearity as an essential resource.

title: Temporal information processing on a 4,500-qubit quantum annealer
summary: Quantum machine learning could uncover statistical structure beyond the reach of classical models, but this requires quantum models large and expressive enough to be useful and cheap enough to read out. Most approaches optimize many quantum parameters and are thus limited by expensive training loops. Here we report a quantum machine-learning model implemented on a programmable superconducting quantum annealer that processes temporal data at large scale using up to 4,500 qubits-the largest quantum machine-learning experiment performed to date. Following the quantum reservoir computing paradigm, the untrained native many-body dynamics generated by reverse annealing is directly used to process temporal data. We prove that the interactions produced during annealing are indispensable-a non-interacting reservoir retains no memory of its input. We evaluate our model experimentally on standard memory benchmarks and demonstrate that it can successfully forecast chaotic time series. These results establish quantum annealers as a scalable platform for large-scale quantum machine learning.

AI.tldr: A quantum reservoir computing model on a programmable superconducting annealer uses untrained many-body dynamics from reverse annealing with up to 4,500 qubits—the largest quantum ML experiment to date—to process temporal data and forecast chaotic time series.
AI.motivation: Quantum machine learning could reveal statistical structure beyond classical models, but requires large, expressive quantum models that are also cheap to read out. Most approaches optimize many quantum parameters, incurring expensive training loops.
AI.method: Following quantum reservoir computing, the model exploits untrained native many-body dynamics generated by reverse annealing, avoiding parameter optimization. It is implemented on a programmable superconducting quantum annealer, using up to 4,500 qubits for temporal data processing. The authors also prove the necessity of annealing-induced interactions for memory retention.
AI.result: Experimentally evaluated on standard memory benchmarks, the model performs successfully and can forecast chaotic time series. The proof shows a non-interacting reservoir retains no memory of its input.
AI.conclusion: Quantum annealers constitute a scalable platform for large-scale quantum machine learning.

title: Quantum tree networks: complete semidefinite hierarchies and the source-transfer model
summary: Understanding the capabilities and limits of quantum systems is central to quantum information processing. This includes determining which correlations can arise in networks of quantum systems distributed by independent sources. Yet for general quantum networks, no systematic, dimension-free method is known to bound these correlations arbitrarily well. We resolve this problem for all quantum tree networks through a new source-transfer model, which we prove equivalent to a mixed quantum model. The mixed model places no restriction on dimension and reduces to the standard tensor-product model in finite dimensions; the source-transfer model instead describes these correlations through states on $C^*$-algebras and completely positive maps composed recursively along the tree. We prove the equivalence by reconstructing local measurements as Radon-Nikodym derivatives in the spatial tensor products prescribed by the network. Building on this characterization, we establish two convergent outer hierarchies of semidefinite programs (SDPs): a novel source-transfer hierarchy and the inflation-NPA hierarchy. For the source-transfer hierarchy, we extend noncommutative real algebraic geometry to multi-state polynomials with completely positive maps, prove a reconstruction theorem establishing its convergence, and give a sufficient stopping criterion for extracting finite-dimensional realizations. For the inflation-NPA hierarchy, we reconstruct source-transfer realizations from weak-operator limits of averages over source copies. Consequently, the game-value promise problem for quantum tree networks in the mixed model is $\mathsf{coRE}$-complete.

AI.tldr: The paper solves the problem of bounding correlations in general quantum tree networks via a new source-transfer model proven equivalent to a dimension-free mixed quantum model, yielding two convergent SDP hierarchies and a coRE-completeness result.
AI.motivation: Understanding the capabilities and limits of quantum systems is central to quantum information processing, including determining which correlations can arise in networks of quantum systems distributed by independent sources. For general quantum networks, no systematic, dimension-free method was known to bound these correlations arbitrarily well.
AI.method: The authors introduce a source-transfer model describing tree-network correlations via states on C*-algebras and completely positive maps composed recursively along the tree, and prove it equivalent to a mixed quantum model (dimension-free, reducing to the tensor-product model in finite dimensions). Equivalence is proven by reconstructing local measurements as Radon-Nikodym derivatives in the network's spatial tensor products. They build two convergent outer hierarchies of SDPs: a novel source-transfer hierarchy and the inflation-NPA hierarchy.
AI.result: For the source-transfer hierarchy, noncommutative real algebraic geometry is extended to multi-state polynomials with completely positive maps, a reconstruction theorem establishes convergence, and a sufficient stopping criterion is given for extracting finite-dimensional realizations. For the inflation-NPA hierarchy, source-transfer realizations are reconstructed from weak-operator limits of averages over source copies.
AI.conclusion: The paper resolves the bounding problem for all quantum tree networks and shows that the game-value promise problem for quantum tree networks in the mixed model is coRE-complete.

title: Observing and evading quantum back-action on a kilogram-scale oscillator
comment: Main text 8 pages, 4 figures. Supplementary 10 pages, 7 figures
summary: Continuous quantum displacement measurements are fundamentally limited by a trade-off between readout imprecision and measurement back-action, constrained by the Heisenberg uncertainty principle. In the Laser Interferometric Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO), these two quantum noise components dominate much of the observation band, making it an excellent testbed. We induce a sub-Hz-linewidth optomechanical mode by trapping the differential motion of the 40-kg mirrors in a band where radiation-pressure back-action dominates the motion. Engineering the quantum state entering the dark port creates correlations between imprecision and back-action that partially cancel their contributions, reducing observed motion near resonance by ~47%. A framework resolving the imprecision, back-action, and correlation terms identifies the origin of this suppression. These results demonstrate quantum back-action evasion and quantum reservoir engineering in a macroscopic optomechanical system.

AI.tldr: Quantum back-action evasion and quantum reservoir engineering are demonstrated in LIGO's 40-kg mirror system: by engineering the squeezed quantum state injected into the dark port, imprecision and back-action correlations partially cancel, suppressing observed mirror motion near resonance by ~47%.
AI.motivation: Continuous quantum displacement measurements face a fundamental trade-off between readout imprecision and measurement back-action set by Heisenberg uncertainty. In LIGO, these quantum noise components dominate much of the observation band, making it an ideal testbed for investigating and evading back-action.
AI.method: The differential motion of the 40-kg mirrors is trapped to induce a sub-Hz-linewidth optomechanical mode in a regime where radiation-pressure back-action dominates the motion. The quantum state entering the dark port is engineered to create correlations between imprecision and back-action that partially cancel their contributions. A framework is introduced to resolve the imprecision, back-action, and correlation terms.
AI.result: Observed motion near resonance is reduced by ~47%. The imprecision/back-action/correlation framework identifies the origin of this suppression, confirming partial cancellation via engineered correlations.
AI.conclusion: These results demonstrate quantum back-action evasion and quantum reservoir engineering in a macroscopic optomechanical system, validating the technique for reducing quantum noise in LIGO-type detectors.

title: Transformers as Intrinsic Optimizers for Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm
summary: The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) is a leading variational framework for combinatorial optimization on noisy intermediate-scale quantum hardware, but its practical performance depends strongly on the classical optimizer used to train its variational parameters. This outer-loop optimization is often nonconvex, initialization-sensitive, and costly when repeated across large families of related problem instances. In this work, we propose a Transformer-based intrinsic optimization framework for QAOA, in which the optimizer itself is learned and embedded directly into the hybrid quantum-classical loop. The proposed graph-conditioned Transformer processes problem structure, current QAOA parameters, measurement feedback, and recent optimization history to predict the next variational-parameter update, thereby reformulating instance-wise classical optimization as an amortized learned policy. We develop a mathematical formulation of this intrinsic-optimization perspective and evaluate the method on QAOA-based MaxCut benchmarks across multiple problem settings, with comparisons against representative classical and learned optimization baselines. The results demonstrate that Transformer-based intrinsic optimization can provide a structured and transferable mechanism for improving the classical component of hybrid quantum optimization algorithms.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Transformer-based intrinsic optimization framework for QAOA, where the classical outer-loop optimizer is replaced by a learned, graph-conditioned policy that predicts variational-parameter updates, evaluated on MaxCut benchmarks.
AI.motivation: QAOA's practical performance depends heavily on its classical outer-loop optimizer, which is nonconvex, initialization-sensitive, and expensive to re-run across many related instances. This motivates amortizing that optimization into a learned policy.
AI.method: A graph-conditioned Transformer is embedded in the hybrid quantum-classical loop. It consumes problem structure, current QAOA parameters, measurement feedback, and recent optimization history to predict the next variational-parameter update, reformulating instance-wise classical optimization as an amortized learned policy. A mathematical formulation of the intrinsic-optimization perspective is developed.
AI.result: Evaluated on QAOA-based MaxCut benchmarks across multiple problem settings and compared against representative classical and learned optimization baselines, the method shows that Transformer-based intrinsic optimization can provide a structured and transferable mechanism for improving the classical component of hybrid quantum optimization.
AI.conclusion: Learned, Transformer-based intrinsic optimization offers a transferable and structured way to improve the classical optimizer in hybrid quantum optimization algorithms such as QAOA.

title: Fifty Years of the GKLS Master Equation: Foundations and Early Developments
comment: To be published in the special volume of OSID dedicated to the 50th anniversary of the GKLS master equation
summary: The year 2026 marks the fiftieth anniversary of the two seminal papers in which Gorini, Kossakowski, and Sudarshan, and independently Lindblad, characterized the generators of completely positive quantum dynamical semigroups. We revisit the conceptual and historical route leading to the Gorini-Kossakowski-Lindblad-Sudarshan (GKLS) master equation and examine several of its early developments and consequences. Our aim is to show how several initially separate mathematical and physical ideas converged in the GKLS structure theorem, imme- diately opening the way to manifold consequences for the description of dissipative quantum phenomena and how that theorem, fifty years later, remains both a foundational result and an active framework for open quantum dynamics.

AI.tldr: A review commemorating the 50th anniversary of the GKLS theorem, tracing the conceptual and historical path to the GKLS master equation and surveying its early developments and lasting role in open quantum dynamics.
AI.motivation: The year 2026 marks fifty years since the independent characterization of generators of completely positive quantum dynamical semigroups by Gorini-Kossakowski-Sudarshan and by Lindblad, providing an occasion to revisit how separate mathematical and physical ideas converged.
AI.method: Historical and conceptual reconstruction: the paper retraces the intellectual route leading to the GKLS structure theorem and examines several of its early developments and consequences.
AI.result: The analysis shows that several initially separate mathematical and physical ideas converged in the GKLS structure theorem, which immediately opened manifold consequences for describing dissipative quantum phenomena.
AI.conclusion: Fifty years on, the GKLS theorem remains both a foundational result and an active framework for open quantum dynamics.

title: Scalable Simulation of Quantum Dynamics on Topological Quantum Hardware
summary: Quantum computers offer a significant advantage in simulating quantum systems compared to classical computers for certain problems, although most current applications are limited to calculating static molecular properties using hybrid quantum-classical hardware. In this work, we establish a framework for the representation of quantum dynamics in molecular and condensed matter systems, designed for execution on topological quantum hardware. By leveraging the non-Abelian braiding statistics of Fibonacci and Ising anyons, we utilize the Solovay-Kitaev algorithm to approximate unitary propagators for a range of systems. We demonstrate the efficacy of these algorithms across a hierarchy of complexity, from two-level systems and one dimensional double-well potentials to condensed phase spin-boson models, simple molecules, and molecular reaction kinetics. These algorithms provide a scalable and robust pathway for simulating many-body condensed phase chemical physics on fault-tolerant quantum devices.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a framework for simulating quantum dynamics in molecular and condensed matter systems on topological quantum hardware, using non-Abelian anyon braiding and the Solovay-Kitaev algorithm to approximate unitary propagators across increasing complexity.
AI.motivation: Most current quantum computing applications for simulating quantum systems are restricted to static molecular properties on hybrid quantum-classical hardware. There is a need for a scalable and robust approach to simulate quantum dynamics of many-body condensed-phase chemical physics.
AI.method: The authors leverage the non-Abelian braiding statistics of Fibonacci and Ising anyons and employ the Solovay-Kitaev algorithm to approximate unitary propagators for a hierarchy of systems.
AI.result: The algorithms are demonstrated across a hierarchy of complexity, ranging from two-level systems and one-dimensional double-well potentials to condensed-phase spin-boson models, simple molecules, and molecular reaction kinetics.
AI.conclusion: These algorithms provide a scalable and robust pathway for simulating many-body condensed-phase chemical physics on fault-tolerant quantum devices.

authors: Julio C. Magdalena de la Fuente
title: Efficiently estimating failure rates of fault-tolerant logical non-Clifford blocks
summary: Useful quantum computation requires the fault-tolerant implementations of a universal gate set which are generically not efficiently simulable. We devise an algebraic framework that allows for efficient sampling from the measurement distribution of fault-tolerant circuits that implement diagonal logic gates in the third level of the Clifford hierarchy. Upon successful sampling we also provide sufficient conditions for decoding success. The resulting estimate for the logical failure rate is an overestimate, which becomes more accurate for blocks that are fault tolerant against arbitrary local errors. The non-Clifford simulation overhead is independent of the number of logical qubits, making the method particularly attractive for large-scale simulations. The framework is based on viewing the non-Clifford gates in the circuit as a cohomology invariant of an underlying spacetime fault complex. The method can also be interfaced with Clifford simulators to simulate larger fault-tolerant circuits and algorithmic subroutines.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an algebraic framework for efficiently sampling the measurement distribution of fault-tolerant circuits implementing diagonal logic gates in the third level of the Clifford hierarchy, enabling estimation of logical failure rates with non-Clifford simulation overhead independent of logical qubit count.
AI.motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires universal gate sets that are generically not efficiently simulable, creating a need for efficient simulation methods for fault-tolerant circuits implementing non-Clifford gates.
AI.method: An algebraic framework treating non-Clifford gates as a cohomology invariant of an underlying spacetime fault complex, combined with sampling from the measurement distribution and sufficient conditions for decoding success. The method can be interfaced with Clifford simulators for larger circuits.
AI.result: Efficient sampling is achieved, and the resulting logical failure rate estimate is an overestimate that becomes more accurate for blocks fault-tolerant against arbitrary local errors. The non-Clifford simulation overhead is independent of the number of logical qubits.
AI.conclusion: The framework is particularly attractive for large-scale simulations of fault-tolerant circuits implementing diagonal logic gates in the third level of the Clifford hierarchy, and can be combined with Clifford simulators to simulate larger fault-tolerant circuits and algorithmic subroutines.

title: Engineering and Probing a One-Dimensional Dipolar Spin Ensemble in Diamond
summary: Dimensionality plays a central role in determining the collective behavior of interacting quantum systems. Engineering strongly interacting ensembles of solid-state spin defects in reduced dimensions remains a significant challenge at the interface between the applied and fundamental sciences. Here, we create and characterize a positionally disordered, quasi-one-dimensional spin chain in diamond, consisting of optically dark substitutional nitrogen defects (P1 centers) and optically addressable probe nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers. Our approach exploits the preferential incorporation of nitrogen along step bunches formed during chemical vapor deposition to achieve both lateral and vertical confinement. Combining spatially resolved materials characterization with nanoscale quantum sensing, we establish the one-dimensional character of the optically dark, unpolarized P1 spin ensemble. We then use correlation spectroscopy to probe local spin autocorrelations and investigate infinite-temperature dipolar spin transport. Our results establish a materials-based route for engineering low-dimensional quantum spin systems.

AI.tldr: The authors engineer a positionally disordered quasi-1D spin chain in diamond by exploiting preferential nitrogen incorporation along step bunches during CVD growth, using NV centers as probes of dark P1 spins.
AI.motivation: Dimensionality governs collective behavior in interacting quantum systems, but engineering strongly interacting ensembles of solid-state spin defects in reduced dimensions remains a major challenge bridging applied and fundamental science.
AI.method: Preferential nitrogen incorporation along step bunches formed during chemical vapor deposition achieves lateral and vertical confinement, yielding a quasi-1D chain of dark substitutional nitrogen (P1) defects with optically addressable NV probe centers. Spatially resolved materials characterization combined with nanoscale quantum sensing establishes the 1D character of the unpolarized P1 ensemble, and correlation spectroscopy probes local spin autocorrelations and infinite-temperature dipolar spin transport.
AI.result: The quasi-1D character of the optically dark, unpolarized P1 spin ensemble is confirmed, and local spin autocorrelations plus infinite-temperature dipolar spin transport are measured via correlation spectroscopy.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a materials-based route for engineering low-dimensional quantum spin systems.

title: Normalizing Flow-Based Bayesian Parameter Estimation for Noisy Quantum States
summary: To extract complete information about experimental noisy quantum states, as well as correlations among different physical parameters, we develop an efficient machine learning-assisted framework with the normalizing flow based Bayesian parameter estimation (BPE). By embedding a physically interpretable parameter vector, ${s}$, into the quantum state ansatzes, $ρ({s})$, the corresponding parameter distribution $p({s}|D)$ is induced from BPE, based on the available experimental data $D$. The BPE allows us to perform parameter correlation analyses, providing powerful insights about how experimental parameters and related noise sources affect quantum features of the system. As an example, the flexibility of our framework is demonstrated using two different physical ansatzes on the optical cat state experiments, where a noisy single-photon state is added to impure squeezed state. With correlations among the Wigner function negativity, photon-addition fraction, noisy fraction, and pump powers, our framework gives interpretations for complicated experimental mechanisms in generating noisy non-Gaussian states. By leveraging normalizing flow-based neural networks and Bayesian uncertainty estimation, along with physical and experimental constraints incorporated naturally, the valuable information inferred in the posterior learning provides guidelines for experimentalists, as well as theorists, in identifying promising parameters to enhance desirable features.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a machine learning-assisted framework combining normalizing flow-based Bayesian parameter estimation (BPE) to extract complete information about experimental noisy quantum states and correlations among physical parameters.
AI.motivation: Extracting complete information about experimental noisy quantum states and correlations among different physical parameters is challenging. The authors aim to provide insights into how experimental parameters and noise sources affect quantum features of the system.
AI.method: A physically interpretable parameter vector s is embedded into quantum state ansatzes ρ(s), and the corresponding parameter distribution p(s|D) is induced via normalizing flow-based Bayesian parameter estimation from experimental data D. This enables parameter correlation analyses. The framework is demonstrated on optical cat state experiments using two different physical ansatzes, where a noisy single-photon state is added to an impure squeezed state.
AI.result: The framework reveals correlations among the Wigner function negativity, photon-addition fraction, noisy fraction, and pump powers, providing interpretations for complicated experimental mechanisms in generating noisy non-Gaussian states.
AI.conclusion: By leveraging normalizing flow-based neural networks and Bayesian uncertainty estimation with natural incorporation of physical and experimental constraints, the posterior learning provides guidelines for experimentalists and theorists to identify promising parameters for enhancing desirable features.

title: Symmetry-driven correlation patterns in one-dimensional periodic fermionic systems: closed-form expressions and exact selection rules for correlation functions, entanglement entropies and mutual information
comment: The following article has been accepted by The Journal of Chemical Physics
summary: We present an analytical study of the spatial structure of correlations in periodic fermionic systems at the single Slater determinant level, focusing on the cyclic case. Exploiting cyclic symmetry, the transformation from localized orbitals to molecular orbitals is simultaneously a discrete Fourier transform, a Vandermonde matrix on the roots of unity, a complex Hadamard matrix, and the character table of the cyclic group $C_m$. Within this framework, the spatial structure of correlations is fully determined by the occupied irreducible representations (Fourier modes), independently of the specific Hamiltonian generating them. In particular, the fermionic two-point correlator is expressed as a truncated Fourier sum over the occupied orbitals, leading to exact analytical expressions for symmetric occupation patterns of Fourier modes ($\ell$ and $-\ell$ pairs), corresponding in quantum chemistry to aromatic fillings, i.e. fillings satisfying Hückel's $4n + 2$ rule. For the half filling case, we derive exact spatial selection rules. In particular, the two-point correlator vanishes identically for all even distances along the ring. This property propagates to reduced density matrices and implies a complete absence of mutual information between the corresponding orbitals. These results reveal that, despite the global delocalization of molecular orbitals, the correlation structure in cyclic systems is highly non-uniform and governed by symmetry-induced interference. Although formulated in terms of cyclic lattice systems, the present results extend straightforwardly to one-dimensional fermionic chains with periodic conditions, reflecting the underlying translational symmetry of the problem. The framework therefore provides a Hamiltonian-independent and universal reference for understanding correlation patterns in one-dimensional periodic fermionic systems.

AI.tldr: The paper analytically studies spatial correlation structure in periodic fermionic systems at the single Slater determinant level, showing that correlations are fully determined by occupied Fourier modes (symmetry) rather than the Hamiltonian, with exact selection rules at half filling.
AI.motivation: Correlation patterns in periodic fermionic systems are typically treated as Hamiltonian-dependent. The authors aim to show that, under cyclic symmetry, the spatial structure of correlations is universal and governed purely by symmetry, providing a Hamiltonian-independent reference framework.
AI.method: Exploiting cyclic symmetry (group $C_m$), the localized-to-molecular orbital transformation is identified simultaneously as a discrete Fourier transform, a Vandermonde matrix on roots of unity, a complex Hadamard matrix, and the character table of $C_m$. The fermionic two-point correlator is expressed as a truncated Fourier sum over occupied irreducible representations (Fourier modes), yielding exact analytical expressions for symmetric ($\ell$, $-\ell$) occupation patterns (aromatic/Hückel $4n+2$ fillings). Half-filling selection rules are derived, and the analysis is propagated to reduced density matrices and mutual information.
AI.result: Exact analytical expressions for the two-point correlator are obtained for symmetric Fourier-mode occupation patterns. At half filling, exact spatial selection rules arise: the two-point correlator vanishes identically at all even distances along the ring. This propagates to reduced density matrices and implies complete absence of mutual information between the corresponding orbitals.
AI.conclusion: Despite global delocalization of molecular orbitals, the correlation structure in cyclic systems is highly non-uniform and governed by symmetry-induced interference. Although formulated for cyclic lattices, the results extend directly to one-dimensional fermionic chains with periodic boundary conditions, providing a Hamiltonian-independent, universal reference for correlation patterns in one-dimensional periodic fermionic systems.

title: A Bi-Objective Routing Framework for Hybrid Terrestrial-Satellite Quantum Networks
summary: Hybrid terrestrial-satellite quantum networks combine terrestrial fiber infrastructure with free-space links to enable long-distance entanglement distribution. Entanglement can be routed over different combinations of terrestrial and satellite links, resulting in paths with different entanglement generation rates (EGRs) and fidelities. Existing routing algorithms, however, typically reduce routing to a single-objective problem by optimizing either EGR or fidelity, or by optimizing one while constraining the other, and thus do not explicitly capture the trade-off between the two. In this paper, we present a bi-objective routing framework for hybrid quantum networks that jointly optimizes end-to-end EGR and fidelity. We formulate routing as a Pareto optimization problem and show that it possesses a special mathematical structure: the bottleneck nature of end-to-end EGR and the multiplicative nature of end-to-end fidelity allow the problem to be transformed into a MAXMIN-MINSUM bi-criterion path problem. This transformation enables the exact polynomial-time computation of a minimal complete Pareto set using Martins' bicriterion routing algorithm. Our results demonstrate that hybrid networks expose substantially richer Pareto frontiers than terrestrial-only networks and that the proposed framework outperforms representative single-objective routing policies by allowing applications to select paths based on their EGR and fidelity requirements.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a bi-objective routing framework for hybrid terrestrial-satellite quantum networks that jointly optimizes end-to-end entanglement generation rate (EGR) and fidelity, transforming the routing problem into a MAXMIN-MINSUM bi-criterion path problem to compute the exact Pareto set in polynomial time.
AI.motivation: Hybrid terrestrial-satellite quantum networks can route entanglement over different combinations of terrestrial and satellite links, yielding paths with varying EGRs and fidelities. Existing routing algorithms collapse this into a single-objective problem (optimizing EGR or fidelity, or one constrained by the other), failing to explicitly capture the trade-off between the two metrics.
AI.method: The authors formulate routing as a Pareto optimization problem that jointly optimizes end-to-end EGR and fidelity. title: Vehicle-Routing Clustering by Sparse Quantum Relaxation
summary: This paper studies the cluster-assignment layer of a cluster-first-route-second decomposition for the capacitated pickup-and-delivery problem with time windows (CPDPTW), instead of a direct route-ordering quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO). We make no quantum-advantage claim. Under strong repair the classical pass alone reaches near-optimal cost at the tested sizes. The result is a regime map linking sparsification, achieved compression, linear-combination-of-unitaries (LCU) 1-norm, heavy-hex two-qubit depth, sampling drift, and final routing quality on Qiskit Aer, calibrated FakeTorino, and IBM Heron ibm_quebec. title: Dephasing-Enhanced Response and Phase Transitions in Quantum Boltzmann Samplers
comment: Main 6 pages + SM 31 pages. Main 3 figures + SM 6 figures
summary: Dephasing can drive a quantum Boltzmann sampler into an ordered phase while its programmed probability distribution remains disordered. We trace this transition to an enhanced conditional response: coherence loss changes how each spin responds to its neighbors, and interactions amplify the change. For all-to-all coupling, we establish the stationary transition at finite dephasing. Near criticality, the magnetization distribution depends on the ratio of dephasing strength to the square root of system size, retaining a finite imprint of coherence even as the local coherent correction vanishes. In the strong-dephasing limit on a square lattice, the dynamics generates effective multispin interactions and probability currents, with Ising-like critical statistics. Adjusting the local dissipative update restores the target probability process on arbitrary graphs.

AI.motivation: Quantum Boltzmann samplers are designed to sample from a target probability distribution, but environmental dephasing (coherence loss) is typically assumed to be a mere nuisance. The paper investigates how dephasing actually reshapes the sampled distribution, potentially pushing the sampler into an ordered phase that no longer matches the programmed disordered distribution—an important reliability concern for quantum sampling devices.

They also analyze the strong-dephasing limit on a square lattice, deriving effective multispin interactions and probability currents with Ising-like critical statistics, and show that adjusting the local dissipative update restores the target process on arbitrary graphs.
