title: A Restricted Boltzmann Machine with Quantum-State Visible Units
summary: We construct a restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM) whose visible input is a quantum state rather than a classical configuration. Each hidden unit carries a trainable quantum template prepared by a parametrized circuit and converts its overlap with the input into a feature. Treating quantum states as high-dimensional continuous visible objects creates nontrivial normalization and scaling problems. We regularize the continuous likelihood and derive two controlled high-dimensional limits, yielding a Hopfield-type network with continuous Hilbert-space patterns and a data-augmented Gram likelihood. The resulting algorithms are compact and use trainable circuit-prepared templates as measurement intermediaries between quantum data and classical optimization. Numerical simulations across several many-body systems demonstrate effective quantum-phase recognition and multicomponent feature extraction.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a restricted Boltzmann machine with quantum states as continuous visible inputs, where hidden units are circuit-prepared quantum templates whose overlap with the input yields features; after deriving controlled high-dimensional limits, it produces compact algorithms for quantum-phase recognition and multicomponent feature extraction in many-body systems.
AI.motivation: Standard RBMs take classical configurations as visible input, so they cannot directly model quantum states, which are high-dimensional continuous objects. Treating quantum states as visible inputs introduces nontrivial normalization and scaling problems that must be addressed.
AI.method: They construct an RBM whose visible input is a quantum state. Each hidden unit holds a trainable quantum template prepared by a parametrized circuit and outputs the overlap with the input as a feature. They regularize the continuous likelihood and derive two controlled high-dimensional limits: a Hopfield-type network with continuous Hilbert-space patterns, and a data-augmented Gram likelihood. The resulting algorithms use circuit-prepared templates as measurement intermediaries between quantum data and classical optimization.

AI.conclusion: A quantum-input RBM with circuit-prepared templates provides a compact framework for learning from quantum states, with the two derived limits offering controlled high-dimensional formulations and showing practical capability in recognizing quantum phases and extracting multiple features.

title: Experimental certification of the nonlocal advantages of quantum imaginarity
comment: [10] pages, [6] figures. Accepted by Physical Review A. DOI: 10.1103/7jcn-yq29
summary: Quantum imaginarity is a distinct resource in quantum information theory, yet its nonlocal properties have not been fully explored. Here, we report an experimental study of the nonlocal advantage of quantum imaginarity (NAQI), in which local measurements on one subsystem can steer the average imaginarity of the conditional states of the other subsystem beyond the corresponding classical bound. The $l_1$-norm of imaginarity inequality is adopted as an experimentally accessible witness. A hybrid optimization algorithm that combines a genetic algorithm with sequential quadratic programming is developed to avoid local optima and accelerate the search for optimal measurement settings. Using polarization-encoded photonic qubits, we prepare two classes of two-qubit Bell-diagonal states and experimentally characterize the imaginarity of the conditional states following local measurements. Clear violations of the $l_1$-norm of imaginarity inequality are observed, providing an experimental certification of NAQI. We further investigate the relationship among NAQI, the nonlocal advantage of quantum coherence (NAQC), and Bell nonlocality based on their respective inequality criteria. For the two-qubit Werner states considered in this work, the regions of states that violate the respective criteria satisfy $\mathcal{D}_{\rm NAQC}\subset\mathcal{D}_{\rm NAQI}\subset\mathcal{D}_{\rm BN}$. Our work provides an experimental realization of NAQI and a comparison of different forms of quantum nonclassicality in a photonic platform.

title: Quantum computers will not be that different: A blueprint for quantum computer architecture at scale
summary: Quantum computers are technologically novel and unusual, but at system scale they should be engineered using many of the same principles that govern classical heterogeneous accelerators. This paper argues that utility-scale quantum architecture is primarily a cost-performance problem across a coupled quantum-classical system, leading to a blueprint for scalable quantum processing unit (QPU) design. Our architecture blueprint is organized around clean logical abstractions, hiding details and complexity of physical qubit modalities below the instruction set architecture (ISA) boundary, and specializes recurring functions aggressively to minimize the cost for utility scale quantum computations. Its low-level implementation through specialized local hardware for control, readout, and quantum error correction (QEC) closely resembles the architecture of high-performance network stacks. One of our main insights is that the design principles and the resulting architecture closely follow established practice from classical computing and networking.

AI.tldr: Utility-scale quantum architecture is framed as a cost-performance problem in a coupled quantum-classical system, yielding a scalable QPU design blueprint with clean ISA-level abstractions and specialized local hardware for control, readout, and QEC that mirrors high-performance network stack architecture.

AI.conclusion: The main insight is that design principles and the resulting architecture closely follow established practice from classical computing and networking, supporting a cost-performance-driven approach to utility-scale quantum architecture.

title: Improving Sample Efficiency in Peptide-HLA Binding Prediction with Hybrid Quantum-Classical Neural Networks
summary: Peptide-HLA binding prediction is a critical step in neoantigen identification for personalized cancer immunotherapy and holds significant clinical value. However, the training data available for many HLA alleles are extremely limited, which severely constrains the performance of conventional methods on this task. Parameterized quantum circuits are hypothesized to induce inductive biases beneficial for learning from small datasets, yet their application to biological sequence prediction remains underexplored. To address this, we propose a hybrid quantum-classical neural network (HQNN) specifically designed for peptide-HLA binding prediction. HQNN integrates multi-source biological feature encoding with parallel quantum feature extractors and a quantum-enhanced classifier. On two HLA alleles (A*02:01 and B*07:02), HQNN outperforms a parameter-matched classical CNN baseline across all training sizes, with the performance gap widening as training data decreases. Ablation studies confirm the respective contributions of the quantum feature extraction module and the quantum classifier. In noise-aware simulations, performance degrades only mildly, and such degradation is reasonable and acceptable under realistic quantum hardware noise levels. These results suggest that hybrid quantum-classical architectures can provide practical sample-efficiency gains for immunoinformatics tasks in low-data regimes.

Evaluation used two HLA alleles (A*02:01 and B*07:02) against a parameter-matched classical CNN baseline across varying training sizes, with ablation studies of the quantum feature extraction module and quantum classifier, plus noise-aware simulations.
AI.result: HQNN outperformed the parameter-matched classical CNN baseline at all training sizes on both alleles, with the gap widening as training data decreased. Ablations confirmed the contributions of both the quantum feature extraction module and the quantum classifier. Under noise-aware simulations, performance degraded only mildly, remaining reasonable and acceptable at realistic quantum hardware noise levels.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid quantum-classical architectures can provide practical sample-efficiency gains for immunoinformatics tasks in low-data regimes.

title: Linear combination of Schrödingerization for quantum linear systems with optimal matrix-query complexity
summary: Quantum linear systems algorithms (QLSAs) aim to solve linear systems $A\bb{x}=\bb{b}$ exponentially faster than classical methods under certain conditions. In this work, we develop quantum algorithms for solving linear algebraic equations from an ODE-based perspective. Inspired by the linear combination of Hamiltonian simulation (LCHS) representation in the Fourier approach \cite{Childs2017QLSA}, we express the solution $\bb{x}$ as a linear combination of solutions to a system of linear convection equations, which become Schrödinger-type equations with unitary evolutions in the Fourier domain. We refer to this representation as LC-Schrödingerization. Based on this result, we construct an LCHS-based quantum algorithm with two LCHS instances: one for time-marching and one for numerical integration. The key construction uses the derivative of a Gaussian-smoothed hat function and recovers the solution over a fixed auxiliary interval. This permits a truncation time independent of the target accuracy and avoids the loss in success probability from selecting a single grid point. Periodization and explicit Fourier coefficients provide the corresponding projection error bounds. Under the stated oracle assumptions and given a constant-factor estimate of the solution norm, direct simulation of the select operators and block preconditioning achieve the optimal matrix-query complexity $\mathcal{O}(κ_A\log\frac1\varepsilon)$ without using variable-time amplitude amplification (VTAA). The same upper bound holds for queries to the right-hand-side preparation oracle.

title: Exact Local Optimality Does Not Compose: The Complexity of Chronological Realization
summary:
The chronological shared realization complexity (CRC) is the smallest normalized stochastic state dimension $C_{\rm seq}$ needed to reproduce a collection of future-response menus using one shared family of controlled transition dynamics. We focus on the rank-tight regime in which both the local realization dimension and the independent-query static carrier width equal $K$, thereby isolating the additional dimensional and computational constraints imposed by chronological consistency. This framework also serves as the classical baseline for state-dimension bounds in sequential quantum processes, where stochastic dynamics generalize to completely positive maps.
  We establish three results in this regime. First, an explicit payload--delay family exhibits an unbounded multiplicative state blow-up: $C_{\rm loc}=C_{\rm stat}=k$ while $C_{\rm seq}=k(L+1)$, isolating the intrinsic state cost of shared temporal pullbacks. Second, for explicitly listed rational finite menus over a fixed five-letter alphabet with a single Boolean terminal effect, exact shared realizability is $\exists\mathbb{R}$-complete, and the zero-versus-inverse-polynomial defect promise problem is $\mathsf{PromiseNP}$-complete, with local and static optima fixed at $K$. Third, a total five-letter chronology compiler translates bounded-rational Intermediate Simplex instances into a polynomially specified regular geometric family over the same fixed alphabet, preserving exact local and static width $K$. The compiled family yields strong $\mathsf{PromiseNP}$-hardness for shared realization on strongly bounded-rational inputs, together with an $\exists\mathbb{R}$ upper bound certified by an exact polynomial-size finite core. Together, these results show that exact local and static optimality need not compose under chronological sharing, even in the rank-tight regime.

The rank-tight regime, where local realization dimension and independent-query static carrier width both equal K, isolates the extra dimensional and computational constraints imposed by chronological consistency. title: Scalable entanglement distribution using encoded hybrid repeater chains
comment: 28 pages main text (plus 14 pages Appendix), 12 figures. Comments are welcome
summary: Long-distance entanglement distribution requires error correction protocols to compensate for qubit decoherence in quantum memories and noise introduced during entanglement swapping. We argue that repeater chains with error-correction capabilities should exploit more than one physical platform, combining the complementary strengths of different quantum memory technologies into a single hybrid repeater architecture. An important constituent of such an architecture is a hybrid repeater which combines type-1 memories, characterized by fast entanglement generation rates and suitability for multiplexing, and type-2 memories that offer long coherence times and low two-qubit gate error rates. Taking the resource-intensive nature of hybrid nodes into account, we propose and analyze repeater chains in which only a subset of nodes need to be hybrid, while the remaining nodes are simpler first-generation repeaters with no error-correction capability. Through detailed Monte Carlo simulations of fault-tolerant encoded repeater chain protocols based on the three-qubit phase-flip repetition code, the $[[7,1,3]]$ Steane code, and the $[[9,1,3]]$ Shor code, we demonstrate that these hybrid architectures outperform pure architectures based on a single memory platform in terms of end-to-end entanglement distribution rate. In our study we develop a full circuit-level noise model of our architectures and examine the impact of an imperfect interface between the two platforms on our hybrid architecture. We also develop a modified version of the swap-as-soon-as-possible policy with multiplexing, more suited to our architecture where some nodes perform error-correction while others do not. This modified policy significantly reduces the information storage time in memory qubits relative to the previously considered swap policies in encoded repeater chains.

AI.tldr: Hybrid quantum repeater architectures combining fast type-1 memories and long-coherence type-2 memories, with only a subset of nodes hybridized, outperform single-platform architectures in end-to-end entanglement distribution rate under circuit-level noise.
AI.motivation: Long-distance entanglement distribution suffers from qubit decoherence in quantum memories and noise during entanglement swapping, requiring error correction. Single-platform repeaters cannot simultaneously provide fast entanglement generation, multiplexing suitability, long coherence times, and low two-qubit gate errors. The paper argues for exploiting complementary strengths of multiple physical platforms in one hybrid repeater architecture.
AI.method: The authors propose hybrid repeater nodes combining type-1 memories (fast entanglement generation, multiplexing suitability) with type-2 memories (long coherence times, low two-qubit gate errors), and analyze chains where only a subset of nodes are hybrid while others are simple first-generation repeaters without error correction. They run detailed Monte Carlo simulations of fault-tolerant encoded repeater chain protocols using the three-qubit phase-flip repetition code, the [[7,1,3]] Steane code, and the [[9,1,3]] Shor code, with a full circuit-level noise model and an imperfect inter-platform interface. They also develop a modified swap-as-soon-as-possible policy with multiplexing suited to chains with mixed error-correcting and non-error-correcting nodes.

The impact of an imperfect interface between the two platforms is examined. The modified swap policy significantly reduces information storage time in memory qubits compared to previously considered swap policies in encoded repeater chains.
AI.conclusion: Combining complementary quantum memory platforms into hybrid repeater chains, even when only a subset of nodes is hybrid, improves entanglement distribution performance. The modified swap-as-soon-as-possible policy with multiplexing is well suited to such architectures and reduces memory storage time, supporting hybrid multi-platform approaches for fault-tolerant quantum repeaters.

title: Transduction-Enabled Superconducting Quantum Repeater: Toward Deterministic Entanglement Distribution with High-Fidelity Gates
summary: Long-distance entanglement distribution is hindered by photon loss in optical fibers and the nocloning theorem. Optical quantum repeater (QR) protocols rely on Bell state measurements (BSMs), they are intrinsically limited to probabilistic photon operations and fail 50% of the time. We propose a hybrid approach to building quantum repeaters that combines the high transmission speed of photonic qubits in optical fiber with the high-fidelity quantum processing capabilities enabled by superconducting circuits. The transduction-enabled superconducting QR (TESQR) architecture eliminates the need for probabilistic BSMs and allows deterministic processing operations. The TESQR framework always yields a final state at the remote nodes rather than aborting on photon loss, manifesting deterministic entanglement distribution within certain parameter regimes. We evaluate the performance by assessing output-state fidelities and success probabilities of entanglement distribution using realistic noise models. Additionally, we integrate an entanglement purification scheme and evaluate the performance through numerical simulations in QuTiP environment. Our results show that, for entanglement swapping, the proposed scheme improves the entanglement distribution rate by an average of 63% and by up to 159% compared with photonic-only architectures. Moreover, after purification, the end-to-end fidelities exceed 0.8 over distances up to 20 km.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the transduction-enabled superconducting quantum repeater (TESQR), a hybrid architecture combining photonic transmission with superconducting processing to achieve deterministic entanglement distribution, improving rates and fidelity over photonic-only repeaters.
AI.motivation: Long-distance entanglement distribution is limited by photon loss in optical fibers and the no-cloning theorem. Existing optical quantum repeater protocols depend on Bell state measurements (BSMs), which are intrinsically probabilistic and fail 50% of the time.
AI.method: A hybrid quantum repeater architecture (TESQR) integrates high-speed photonic qubits in optical fiber with high-fidelity superconducting quantum processing via transduction. It removes the need for probabilistic BSMs, enabling deterministic processing operations. Performance is evaluated using realistic noise models for output-state fidelity and success probability, and an entanglement purification scheme is integrated and simulated numerically in QuTiP.
AI.result: For entanglement swapping, TESQR improves the entanglement distribution rate by an average of 63% and up to 159% versus photonic-only architectures. After purification, end-to-end fidelities exceed 0.8 over distances up to 20 km.
AI.conclusion: The TESQR framework always yields a final state at the remote nodes instead of aborting on photon loss, achieving deterministic entanglement distribution within certain parameter regimes. The hybrid transduction-enabled superconducting approach offers a promising route to higher-rate, high-fidelity long-distance entanglement distribution.

title: 90%-Efficient Optical Storage in a Rare-Earth Crystal with a Low-Loss Impedance-Matched Cavity
summary: High-efficiency optical storage in rare-earth-ion-doped crystals is challenging because of their typically weak optical absorption,which makes cavity-enhanced memories highly sensitive to parasitic intracavity loss. Here we demonstrate a 90.1(5)% storage efficiency for coherent optical pulses in an impedance-matched cavity atomic-frequency-comb memory based on Eu3+:Y2SiO5. The Brewster-angle configuration of the crystal and fully cryogenic Fabry-Pérot cavity reduce the round-trip intracavity loss to 0.37%. Quantitative modeling shows that further improvement is limited primarily by AFC preparation and its associated dispersive response rather than by residual cavity loss,identifying the principal requirements for further approaching unity efficiency.

AI.tldr: A 90.1(5)% storage efficiency for coherent optical pulses is demonstrated in a cryogenic impedance-matched cavity atomic-frequency-comb memory using Eu3+:Y2SiO5, with residual intracavity loss reduced to 0.37%; further improvement is limited mainly by AFC preparation and dispersion, not cavity loss.
AI.motivation: Optical storage in rare-earth-ion-doped crystals suffers from weak optical absorption, making cavity-enhanced memories highly sensitive to parasitic intracavity loss; achieving high-efficiency storage therefore requires minimizing this loss.
AI.method: An impedance-matched cavity atomic-frequency-comb (AFC) memory is implemented in Eu3+:Y2SiO5. A Brewster-angle crystal configuration combined with a fully cryogenic Fabry-Pérot cavity is used to reduce round-trip intracavity loss. Quantitative modeling is employed to analyze the efficiency limits.
AI.result: A storage efficiency of 90.1(5)% for coherent optical pulses is achieved, with round-trip intracavity loss reduced to 0.37%. The modeling shows that further efficiency improvement is constrained primarily by AFC preparation and its associated dispersive response rather than by residual cavity loss.
AI.conclusion: The work identifies AFC preparation and dispersion as the principal remaining bottlenecks, establishing the key requirements for approaching unity storage efficiency in cavity-enhanced rare-earth-ion-doped crystal memories.

title: Local unitary equivalence of orthogonal arrays and related linear codes
summary: Orthogonal arrays (OAs) are combinatorial configurations with applications in experimental design, error-correcting codes, and quantum information. Local unitary (LU) equivalence provides a natural framework for classifying multipartite entangled states. Using the correspondence between OAs and quantum states, Goyeneche and Życzkowski [Phys. Rev. A, 2014, 90: 022316] posed the problem of determining when OAs are $LU$ equivalent. In this paper, we construct OAs from generator matrices and establish conditions for Fourier-based $LU$ equivalence of OAs and irredundant orthogonal arrays (IrOAs). For prime alphabets, we identify the Fourier partners of the linear OAs considered here with the arrays of their corresponding dual codes. This gives an explicit connection between $LU$ equivalence and coding theory. We also identify families of $LU$ equivalent OAs arising from specific classes of linear codes.

AI.tldr: The paper characterizes Fourier-based local unitary (LU) equivalence of orthogonal arrays (OAs) and irredundant OAs by constructing them from generator matrices, and links this, for prime alphabets, to dual codes of linear codes.
AI.motivation: Goyeneche and Życzkowski (PRA 2014) raised the open problem of determining when orthogonal arrays are LU equivalent, in view of the OA-quantum state correspondence and the classification of multipartite entangled states. This work addresses that problem.
AI.method: Construct OAs from generator matrices and establish conditions for Fourier-based LU equivalence of OAs and irredundant OAs (IrOAs). For prime alphabets, identify the Fourier partners of the linear OAs considered with the arrays of their corresponding dual codes, thereby relating LU equivalence to coding theory.

title: Long-horizon autoformalization of a core theorem underlying MIP* = RE
comment: 72 pages. Main text 13 pages with 4 figures and 1 table, followed by supplementary appendices (57 pages, 9 figures, 17 tables) and references. Lean 4 library: https://github.com/LionSR/MIPStarRE
summary: Landmark mathematical formalizations have taken specialist teams years to complete. We present FormalFlow, a system that coordinates AI proving agents under human supervision to address statement drift and proof composition in long-horizon formalization. Drawing on software engineering principles and practices, it uses a shared blueprint to guide nested planning, proving and review loops. Agents strengthen verification and review throughout formalization. We completed a machine-checked Lean 4 proof of the quantum soundness of the classical low individual-degree test, a core theorem underlying MIP* = RE. Developing the proof took 63 days; greater parallelism could further reduce this time. The final library contains 126,367 lines of Lean code, all generated by agents. The formalization corrects side conditions and intermediate errors while preserving the published final error bound under corrected assumptions. This work provides a verified foundation for quantum complexity and demonstrates a route to affordable verification of major research proofs by small teams.

AI.tldr: FormalFlow coordinates AI proving agents under human supervision via a shared blueprint to manage statement drift and proof composition in long-horizon Lean 4 formalization, producing a machine-checked proof of the quantum soundness of the classical low individual-degree test (underlying MIP* = RE) in 63 days with 126,367 lines of agent-generated Lean code.
AI.motivation: Landmark mathematical formalizations have historically required specialist teams working over years, making verification of major research proofs expensive and inaccessible to small teams. Long-horizon formalization also suffers from statement drift and difficulties in composing proofs.
AI.method: FormalFlow coordinates AI proving agents under human supervision. Drawing on software engineering principles, it employs a shared blueprint to guide nested planning, proving, and review loops, with agents strengthening verification and review throughout the formalization process.
AI.result: The system completed a machine-checked Lean 4 proof of the quantum soundness of the classical low individual-degree test in 63 days, with greater parallelism possible to reduce time further. The final library comprises 126,367 lines of Lean code, all agent-generated, and the formalization corrects side conditions and intermediate errors while preserving the published final error bound under corrected assumptions.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a verified foundation for quantum complexity and demonstrates a route to affordable verification of major research proofs by small teams.

title: Automated search for highly contextual Kochen-Specker proofs
summary: Observable-based Kochen-Specker proofs are configurations of multi-qubit Pauli observables grouped into contexts whose products are plus or minus the indentity. Their robustness as state-independent contextuality tests can be measured by the tolerated error per context $\varepsilon = 2d/|H|$, where $d$ is the contextuality degree and $|H|$ the number of contexts. Since the degree depends only on an underlying abstract structure called the hypergram i.e. the pair formed by the context hypergraph and the anticommutation graph, the search for highly contextual proofs can be carried out on them instead, with no reference to qubits or to any particular Pauli labeling. We further exploit this by enumerating anticommutation graphs first, and then by associating to each graph $G$ the single hypergram carrying its entire hypergraph support $HS(G)$, so that exactly one candidate is examined per graph. Applied to the House of Graphs database and to censuses of vertex-transitive graphs on at most 24 vertices, this pipeline recovers the Peres-Mermin square, the doily and the Mermin pentagram, and yields configurations reaching $\varepsilon = 0.707$, against $0.424$ for the previous published record. The best configurations are predominantly those stemming from line graphs and unions of graphs; we explain the former by showing that every perfect matching of a graph is a context of its line graph, which exhibits the Peres-Mermin square and the doily as the first members of two infinite families. We close with finite geometric descriptions of the most striking configurations inside symplectic polar spaces, in terms of ovoids, hyperbolic quadrics and Fano planes.

AI.tldr: This paper develops an observable-based search pipeline for Kochen-Specker proofs by enumerating anticommutation graphs and their hypergrams, finding state-independent contextuality configurations with robustness up to ε = 0.707 versus the previous 0.424, and giving geometric descriptions in symplectic polar spaces.
AI.motivation: Observable-based Kochen-Specker proofs are useful as state-independent contextuality tests, and their robustness is governed by the contextuality degree d and the number of contexts |H|. Since d depends only on the underlying abstract hypergram, the search for highly contextual proofs can be conducted without reference to qubits or Pauli labelings, motivating a graph/hypergraph-based enumeration approach.
AI.method: The authors measure robustness by ε = 2d/|H|. They exploit the fact that the contextuality degree depends only on the hypergram—the context hypergraph together with the anticommutation graph. The search is therefore performed on hypergrams rather than Pauli configurations. They enumerate anticommutation graphs first, then associate to each graph G the single hypergram carrying its entire hypergraph support HS(G), so exactly one candidate is examined per graph. This pipeline is applied to the House of Graphs database and censuses of vertex-transitive graphs on at most 24 vertices. The paper also analyzes line graphs and graph unions, proving that every perfect matching of a graph is a context of its line graph.
AI.result: The pipeline recovers the Peres-Mermin square, the doily, and the Mermin pentagram. It yields configurations reaching ε = 0.707, compared with 0.424 for the previous published record. The best configurations predominantly arise from line graphs and unions of graphs. The Peres-Mermin square and the doily are shown to be the first members of two infinite families. The most striking configurations are given finite geometric descriptions inside symplectic polar spaces in terms of ovoids, hyperbolic quadrics, and Fano planes.
AI.conclusion: Highly robust state-independent contextuality proofs can be found efficiently by searching abstract hypergrams derived from anticommutation graphs, avoiding qubit- or Pauli-specific representations. This yields improved robustness records and reveals structural connections to line graphs, infinite families, and finite symplectic polar space geometry.

title: Quantum WalkScore: Benchmarking Quantum Computers on the Graph Nodefinding Problem
summary: Recent advances in quantum computing hardware toward fault-tolerance have increased interest in evaluating near-term quantum platforms on application-relevant quantum algorithms. In this work, we introduce Quantum WalkScore (QWS), a scalable application-oriented benchmark designed to assess the performance of NISQ and future fault-tolerant quantum computers in executing essential quantum routines --discrete-time quantum walks and quantum amplitude amplification-- to solve the graph nodefinding problem (marked-vertex search). QWS quantifies performance by scoring the largest problem size for which a designated target node can be found with success probability above a defined threshold. In addition to the complete protocol description, we provide example parameter-selection scenarios designed from noiseless simulation results and demonstrate QWS evaluation through experimental runs on multiple generations of IBM real quantum processors.

AI.tldr: QWS is a scalable, application-oriented benchmark that scores NISQ and fault-tolerant quantum computers by the largest graph size for which a marked node can be found above a success-probability threshold using discrete-time quantum walks and amplitude amplification, validated on IBM processors.
AI.motivation: Growing interest in fault-tolerant quantum hardware has created a need to evaluate near-term platforms on application-relevant algorithms rather than only synthetic circuit metrics, motivating a scalable, application-oriented benchmark.
AI.method: The benchmark targets graph nodefinding (marked-vertex search) via discrete-time quantum walks and quantum amplitude amplification. It defines a complete protocol, including parameter-selection scenarios derived from noiseless simulations, and scores performance as the largest problem size at which a designated target node is found with success probability above a set threshold.
AI.result: Example parameter-selection scenarios from noiseless simulations are provided, and QWS evaluation is demonstrated through experimental runs on several generations of IBM real quantum processors.
AI.conclusion: QWS offers a scalable, application-oriented benchmark suited to assessing both NISQ and future fault-tolerant quantum computers on essential quantum routines, with demonstrated practical applicability on real hardware.

title: Quantum Graph Convolutional Networks: Implementation and Trainability Analysis
summary: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) achieve state-of-the-art performance on graph-structured data, but training and inference on large graphs are often bottlenecked by memory constraints and sparse linear-algebra workloads. Quantum computing offers an alternative set of primitives that may improve scalability for graph learning. Building on the quantum graph neural network (QGNN) framework of Liao \textit{et al.}, this work implements two representative architectures --- the Simplified Graph Convolution (SGC) and Linear Graph Convolution (LGC) models --- and evaluates them on open benchmark graph datasets and semi-supervised learning tasks using quantum simulation. We compare predictive performance and optimization behavior against classical baselines, showing that the quantum models achieve competitive performance with fewer parameters. Finally, we present a cost gradient analysis that identifies the tasks for which the models showcased are trainable. This is followed by a classical simulability study to find regimes in which the proposed circuits remain robust during training.

AI.tldr: This work implements Simplified Graph Convolution (SGC) and Linear Graph Convolution (LGC) quantum graph neural network architectures based on the QGNN framework, evaluates them via quantum simulation on benchmark datasets, and finds competitive performance with fewer parameters, along with cost gradient and classical simulability analyses.
AI.motivation: GNNs achieve state-of-the-art performance on graph-structured data, but training and inference on large graphs are bottlenecked by memory constraints and sparse linear-algebra workloads. Quantum computing offers alternative primitives that may improve scalability for graph learning, motivating the exploration of quantum approaches to graph convolution.
AI.method: Building on the quantum graph neural network (QGNN) framework of Liao et al., the authors implement two representative architectures — Simplified Graph Convolution (SGC) and Linear Graph Convolution (LGC) — and evaluate them on open benchmark graph datasets and semi-supervised learning tasks using quantum simulation. They compare predictive performance and optimization behavior against classical baselines, and conduct a cost gradient analysis plus a classical simulability study.
AI.result: The quantum models achieve competitive predictive performance relative to classical baselines while using fewer parameters. A cost gradient analysis identifies the tasks for which the showcased models are trainable, and the classical simulability study identifies regimes in which the proposed circuits remain robust during training.
AI.conclusion: Quantum versions of SGC and LGC are viable, parameter-efficient alternatives for graph learning, with trainability and robustness characterized by cost gradient and classical simulability analyses, delineating the regimes where the proposed circuits remain effective.

title: Semiclassical scaling of eigenstate thermalization in single-particle chaotic systems
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures; Supplemental Material: 3 pages, 1 figure
summary: We study the off-diagonal matrix elements of real-space observables in time-reversal-invariant single-particle chaotic systems. By analyzing the semiclassical expression for the off-diagonal variance derived from Berry's conjecture, we show that the banded structure of the observable matrix emerges naturally. For local observables, we identify a characteristic bandwidth associated with a late-time timescale inversely proportional to the particle velocity. We further show that, for systems with steep-wall confinement, the predicted magnitude follows the entropy scaling of the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis (ETH), multiplied by an additional kinetic-energy-dependent factor that is independent of spatial dimension and is not captured by conventional many-body ETH. We illustrate these results through a case study of quantum billiards and verify the semiclassical scaling numerically in a generalized quarter-Sinai billiard. Our results elucidate the dynamical implications of Berry's conjecture and provide a comparison between single-particle eigenstate thermalization and many-body ETH.

AI.tldr: Off-diagonal matrix elements of real-space observables in single-particle chaotic systems exhibit a natural banded structure; the bandwidth corresponds to a late-time scale inversely proportional to particle velocity, and the magnitude follows ETH entropy scaling times a kinetic-energy-dependent factor.
AI.motivation: Understanding the structure of observable matrix elements in chaotic quantum systems underpins eigenstate thermalization and quantum ergodicity, yet the behavior of off-diagonal elements of real-space observables in single-particle chaotic systems—and its link to Berry's conjecture and banded random matrix structure—remains underexplored.
AI.method: Semiclassical analysis of time-reversal-invariant single-particle chaotic systems, starting from Berry's conjecture to derive the off-diagonal variance of real-space observables; identification of a characteristic bandwidth and timescale; a case study of quantum billiards; and numerical verification in a generalized quarter-Sinai billiard.
AI.result: The banded structure of the observable matrix emerges naturally from the semiclassical off-diagonal variance. For local observables, a characteristic bandwidth appears, tied to a late-time timescale inversely proportional to particle velocity. For steep-wall confinement, the predicted magnitude follows ETH entropy scaling multiplied by an additional kinetic-energy-dependent factor—independent of spatial dimension—not captured by conventional many-body ETH. Numerical results in a generalized quarter-Sinai billiard confirm the semiclassical scaling.
AI.conclusion: The findings clarify the dynamical implications of Berry's conjecture and establish a quantitative comparison between single-particle eigenstate thermalization and many-body ETH, highlighting a distinctive kinetic-energy-dependent correction absent in conventional formulations.

title: Private communication from Pauli channels with no privacy
summary: A channel capacity quantifies the communication capability of a noisy physical process. In contrast to communication channels in the classical world, quantum theory makes this capability contextual. We show that two Pauli two-qubit channels, each with zero private classical capacity, can be used to transmit private information when used together. One is a two-qubit Pauli channel whose environment can reconstruct the receiver output up to matrix transposition; the other is an antidegradable channel. We obtain a similar result when the second channel is the 50% qubit erasure channel. A simple binary code built from rank-three mixtures of Bell states activates private communication. The main ingredient in our construction is a transpose-antidegradable channel that is not antidegradable.

AI.tldr: Two quantum channels, each individually having zero private classical capacity, can jointly transmit private information. This demonstrates superactivation of private capacity using Pauli channels and a transpose-antidegradable channel.
AI.motivation: Classical channel capacity is additive in the sense that channel capability is a fixed property. Quantum theory makes communication capability contextual, suggesting that combining channels with individually zero private capacity might enable private communication. The authors aim to demonstrate this superactivation phenomenon.
AI.method: Construct two Pauli two-qubit channels: one whose environment can reconstruct the receiver output up to matrix transposition, and either an antidegradable channel or the 50% qubit erasure channel. Use a simple binary code built from rank-three mixtures of Bell states.
AI.result: Both channels individually have zero private classical capacity, yet when used together they transmit private information. The key ingredient is a transpose-antidegradable channel that is not antidegradable, enabling private communication superactivation.
AI.conclusion: Private classical capacity of quantum channels exhibits superactivation: channels with zero private capacity individually can jointly enable private communication. The construction relies on a transpose-antidegradable channel that is not antidegradable.

title: Electrostatic Stabilization of Near-Surface Quantum Sensors via Dielectric Interface Engineering
summary: Control of charge-state stability in near-surface quantum defects is critical for nanoscale sensing, yet remains particularly challenging under ultra-high vacuum (UHV), where surface-induced band bending destabilizes the metrologically relevant charge-state. Here, we present a robust and reproducible approach for stabilizing shallowly implanted (< 10 nm deep) nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in near-UHV conditions (P = $3 \times 10^{-9}$ mbar) based on dielectric interface engineering. Through measurements on individually addressable NV centers, we demonstrate that a TiO2 coating on the diamond suppresses surface-induced electrostatic fields, yielding a 79% increase n NV- population and a 45% enhancement in NV-spin resonance contrast at room temperature. Coherent control measurements further reveal suppressed charge-state conversion dynamics. These results establish dielectric screening as a powerful and reproducible strategy to engineer charge transition energetics of NV centers in scanning-probe-compatible geometries under extreme conditions.

AI.tldr: Dielectric interface engineering via a TiO2 coating on diamond stabilizes near-surface NV centers under UHV, increasing NV- population by 79% and spin-resonance contrast by 45% at room temperature.
AI.motivation: Charge-state stability of near-surface quantum defects is crucial for nanoscale sensing but is difficult to maintain under ultra-high vacuum (UHV), where surface-induced band bending destabilizes the metrologically relevant charge state. A robust, reproducible stabilization approach is needed for scanning-probe-compatible geometries.
AI.method: Shallowly implanted (<10 nm deep) NV centers in diamond were studied under near-UHV conditions (P = 3×10⁻⁹ mbar). Dielectric interface engineering was implemented by applying a TiO2 coating, and measurements were performed on individually addressable NV centers, including spin-resonance and coherent control measurements.
AI.result: The TiO2 coating suppressed surface-induced electrostatic fields, yielding a 79% increase in NV- population and a 45% enhancement in NV spin-resonance contrast at room temperature. Coherent control measurements further revealed suppressed charge-state conversion dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Dielectric screening is established as a powerful and reproducible strategy to engineer the charge transition energetics of NV centers in scanning-probe-compatible geometries under extreme conditions.

title: Exceptional points and Jordan-chain signatures in quantum first-passage statistics
summary: Exceptional-point signatures in first-passage observables are governed by two independent survival mechanisms: nonlinear spectral defectivity must pass from the one-record or transfer description to the physical one-level first-passage ladder, and the resulting ladder Jordan mode must have nonzero overlap with the chosen preparation and terminal observation. For finite reset-form monitored quantum systems with upward-skip-free counting, we prove the exact threshold factorization $H_N(s)=R_s^N$, identify the physical Perron branch, and derive the transfer factorization $Q_s(r)=B_s(r)(R_s-rI)$. Invertibility of the cofactor gives local equality of Smith data, whereas a singular cofactor can contribute transfer multiplicity absent from the ladder. An order-two Keldysh formula yields an independent observation gate. We then prove a fixed-reset no-go theorem: even a defective full tilted generator cannot generate a cumulative-count Jordan polynomial when the post-count ladder is scalar. Finally, we construct a three-reset monitored-Lindblad witness, minimal within irreducible nonnegative ladders, with a genuine subleading $Nλ^N$ threshold term and a coherence-tuned model in which a binary terminal effect retains the exact polynomial signature at a transversal transform-domain exceptional point. The analysis is formulated at the level of exact transform-domain structure; time-domain asymptotics and perturbative robustness remain separate questions.

AI.tldr: Exceptional-point (EP) signatures in first-passage observables require two independent survival mechanisms: (i) nonlinear spectral defectivity must propagate from the one-record/transfer description into the physical one-level first-passage ladder, and (ii) the resulting ladder Jordan mode must have nonzero overlap with both the preparation and the terminal observation. For finite reset-form monitored quantum systems with upward-skip-free counting, the authors prove the threshold factorization H_N(s)=R_s^N, identify the physical Perron branch, and derive Q_s(r)=B_s(r)(R_s-rI); a singular cofactor can add transfer multiplicity absent from the ladder. A fixed-reset no-go theorem is proven, and a minimal three-reset monitored-Lindblad witness is constructed exhibiting a genuine subleading Nλ^N threshold term.
AI.motivation: Exceptional points are widely invoked to explain anomalous first-passage and counting statistics, but their appearance in observable quantities is often asserted rather than derived. The paper aims to clarify exactly which structural conditions are required for EP defectivity to actually manifest as a genuine polynomial (Jordan-type) signature in first-passage observables, distinguishing true physical signatures from artifacts of the transfer or one-record description.
AI.method: The analysis is carried out at the level of exact transform-domain structure for finite reset-form monitored quantum systems with upward-skip-free counting. The authors prove the threshold factorization H_N(s)=R_s^N, identify the physical Perron branch, and derive the transfer factorization Q_s(r)=B_s(r)(R_s-rI). They analyze the invertibility of the cofactor to relate Smith data and transfer multiplicity, employ an order-two Keldysh formula as an independent observation gate, prove a fixed-reset no-go theorem, and construct a three-reset monitored-Lindblad witness plus a coherence-tuned model at a transversal transform-domain exceptional point.
AI.result: Invertibility of the cofactor gives local equality of Smith data, while a singular cofactor can contribute transfer multiplicity absent from the ladder. The order-two Keldysh formula yields an independent observation gate. The fixed-reset no-go theorem shows that even a defective full tilted generator cannot generate a cumulative-count Jordan polynomial when the post-count ladder is scalar. A minimal three-reset monitored-Lindblad witness (minimal within irreducible nonnegative ladders) is constructed with a genuine subleading Nλ^N threshold term, and a coherence-tuned model retains the exact polynomial signature at a transversal transform-domain exceptional point.
AI.conclusion: EP signatures in first-passage observables are governed by two independent survival mechanisms: nonlinear spectral defectivity must pass into the physical one-level first-passage ladder, and the ladder Jordan mode must have nonzero overlap with both preparation and terminal observation. The results are formulated at the level of exact transform-domain structure; time-domain asymptotics and perturbative robustness remain separate, open questions.

title: Rydberg quantum antennas for chip-interfaced single-photon source array
summary: We propose a Rydberg quantum antenna, consisting of a one-dimensional chain of neutral atoms trapped in a standing-wave optical tweezer, as a chip-interfaced single-photon source. Rydberg blockade induces a single collective excitation in the atomic chain, while its ordered geometry shapes the photon emission into a directional beam, thereby realizing a quantum antenna that emits strictly one photon at a time. Through numerical simulations, we demonstrate single-photon collection efficiencies into a waveguide exceeding 70\% through a high-NA lens with a negligible multiple excitation probability. These performance are robust against probabilistic atom loading in the standing-wave dipole traps, requiring only ten atoms, indicating experimental feasibility. The Rydberg quantum antenna thus offers a unique route toward scalable arrays of high-efficiency, high-purity, and identical single-photon sources interfaced with a photonic chip, addressing key challenges in photonic quantum information technology.

AI.tldr: A Rydberg quantum antenna made of a 1D trapped-atom chain acts as a chip-interfaced single-photon source: Rydberg blockade yields one collective excitation and the ordered geometry gives directional emission, reaching >70% single-photon collection into a waveguide with negligible multi-excitation probability and robustness requiring only ~10 atoms.
AI.motivation: Photonic quantum information technology needs scalable, high-efficiency, high-purity, and identical single-photon sources that can be interfaced with a photonic chip; meeting these requirements simultaneously remains a key challenge.
AI.method: Propose a Rydberg quantum antenna: a 1D chain of neutral atoms trapped in a standing-wave optical tweezer. Rydberg blockade creates a single collective excitation in the chain, and the ordered geometry directs photon emission into a directional beam. Performance assessed via numerical simulations, including collection into a waveguide through a high-NA lens and robustness to probabilistic atom loading.
AI.result: Numerical simulations show single-photon collection efficiencies into a waveguide exceeding 70% through a high-NA lens, with negligible multiple-excitation probability. Performance is robust against probabilistic atom loading in the standing-wave dipole traps and requires only ten atoms.
AI.conclusion: The Rydberg quantum antenna provides a unique route to scalable arrays of high-efficiency, high-purity, identical single-photon sources interfaced with a photonic chip, addressing key challenges in photonic quantum information technology and indicating experimental feasibility.

title: QECirc: A Community-Driven, FAIR Library of Quantum Error Correction Circuits
summary: Quantum error correction (QEC) underpins fault-tolerant quantum computing, but the circuits that realize QEC codes (encoders, logical state-preparation and gate routines, and syndrome-extraction schedules) are scattered across papers and one-off repositories in incompatible formats, often documented too sparsely to reconstruct or reuse. We present QECirc (https://qecirc.com/), a community-driven, open library that makes QEC circuits Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR). Each entry links to its underlying code, ships in Stim and OpenQASM with interactive visualizations, and is checked for correctness before publication. In short, where a catalog such as the Error Correction Zoo describes the codes, QECirc provides the concrete circuits that realize them.

AI.tldr: QECirc is a community-driven open library offering standardized, verified quantum error correction circuits in Stim and OpenQASM formats with interactive visualizations, complementing code catalogs like the Error Correction Zoo.
AI.motivation: QEC circuits (encoders, logical state preparation, gate routines, syndrome extraction) are scattered across papers and one-off repositories in incompatible formats, often too sparsely documented to reconstruct or reuse, hindering fault-tolerant quantum computing development.
AI.method: QECirc provides a curated, open, community-driven library where each circuit entry links to its underlying code, is distributed in Stim and OpenQASM, includes interactive visualizations, and undergoes correctness checks before publication.
AI.result: The library makes QEC circuits Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR), with verified and standardized circuit entries available at https://qecirc.com/.
AI.conclusion: Whereas catalogs like the Error Correction Zoo describe QEC codes, QECirc supplies the concrete, reusable circuits that realize them, supporting fault-tolerant quantum computing.

title: Fast Unitary Preparation of Surface-Code Logical States on Neutral-Atom Hardware
summary: Preparing logical states is a constantly recurring primitive at the start of any surface-code-based quantum computation. The standard measurement-based protocol is expensive on neutral atoms, since measurements are orders of magnitude slower than gates and, on single-zone architectures, additionally require shuttling the atoms to a readout zone. In this work, we present a measurement-free, unitary preparation of surface-code Pauli eigenstates tailored to neutral atoms. A bidirectional stabilizer-expanding CNOT cascade grows the patch from its middle line outward in depth $(d{+}3)/2$, while retaining fault distance $d$ in the protected error direction. Each layer maps to one collective atom move followed by a single global Rydberg pulse, with about one row pickup per two layers. We compile and simulate the resulting schedules with the open-source bloqade toolchain under a hardware-calibrated, circuit-level neutral-atom noise model. The bidirectional cascade achieves the lowest logical error rate at every distance, and is the only construction tested that operates below threshold for both logical states at the considered device-level noise.

AI.tldr: A measurement-free, unitary method for preparing surface-code Pauli eigenstates on neutral atoms, using a bidirectional stabilizer-expanding CNOT cascade that grows the patch from its middle line outward and maps each layer to a collective atom move plus a global Rydberg pulse.
AI.motivation: Standard measurement-based surface-code logical-state preparation is expensive on neutral atoms, because measurements are orders of magnitude slower than gates and single-zone architectures require shuttling atoms to a readout zone.
AI.method: A bidirectional stabilizer-expanding CNOT cascade grows the code patch from its middle line outward in depth (d+3)/2 while retaining fault distance d in the protected error direction. Each layer corresponds to one collective atom move followed by a single global Rydberg pulse, with about one row pickup per two layers. Schedules are compiled and simulated with the open-source bloqade toolchain under a hardware-calibrated, circuit-level neutral-atom noise model.
AI.result: The bidirectional cascade achieves the lowest logical error rate at every distance and is the only tested construction operating below threshold for both logical states at the considered device-level noise.
AI.conclusion: The proposed measurement-free unitary preparation is well suited to neutral-atom hardware, offering fault-distance-preserving, low-error logical-state preparation without measurement or shuttling overhead.

title: Transformer fault diagnosis using an efficient simulation-driven variational quantum classifier with domain-aware feature encoding
comment: This paper has been published in Alexandria Engineering Journal. Please cite the published version
summary: Early transformer fault diagnosis is challenged by nonlinear dissolved-gas interactions, overlapping fault signatures, and limited labeled data, while practical deployment further requires reliable performance under realistic computational constraints. This paper presents a simulation-driven modeling framework for dissolved gas analysis-based transformer fault diagnosis, in which a carefully engineered variational quantum classifier (VQC) is employed as the computational core and systematically analyzed through simulation. The framework integrates domain-aware feature modeling derived from Duval geometry with a lightweight two-qubit quantum representation, enabling nonlinear gas-interaction effects to be captured within a shallow parameterized circuit. A hybrid ZX-YY quantum feature map is designed to model non-commuting feature interactions, while a full-entanglement EfficientSU2 ansatz provides adequate expressive capacity under strict resource limits. Model behavior is evaluated using a comprehensive simulation pipeline including noise-aware circuit emulation, cross-dataset validation, and limited hardware-in-the-loop execution, allowing key effects of circuit depth, noise, and optimization strategy to be examined. Simulation results on benchmark dissolved-gas-analysis datasets demonstrate high diagnostic accuracy, strong generalization capability, and robustness to realistic noise levels with minimal quantum resources. The results highlight the effectiveness of simulation-informed modeling for practical transformer diagnostic applications, offering a reproducible and resource-efficient pathway for evaluating quantum-enhanced fault diagnosis methods.

AI.tldr: A simulation-driven variational quantum classifier (VQC) framework for dissolved gas analysis-based transformer fault diagnosis, using Duval-geometry features and a compact two-qubit circuit to achieve high accuracy and noise robustness with minimal quantum resources.
AI.motivation: Early transformer fault diagnosis faces nonlinear dissolved-gas interactions, overlapping fault signatures, and limited labeled data. Practical deployment additionally demands reliable performance under realistic computational constraints, motivating resource-efficient diagnostic modeling.
AI.method: The paper develops a simulation-driven modeling framework with a carefully engineered VQC as the computational core. It integrates domain-aware feature modeling from Duval geometry with a lightweight two-qubit quantum representation. A hybrid ZX-YY quantum feature map captures non-commuting feature interactions, and a full-entanglement EfficientSU2 ansatz supplies expressive capacity under strict resource limits. Evaluation uses a comprehensive simulation pipeline with noise-aware circuit emulation, cross-dataset validation, and limited hardware-in-the-loop execution, examining circuit depth, noise, and optimization strategy.
AI.result: On benchmark dissolved-gas-analysis datasets, simulation results show high diagnostic accuracy, strong generalization, and robustness to realistic noise levels while using minimal quantum resources.
AI.conclusion: Simulation-informed modeling is effective for practical transformer diagnostics, providing a reproducible and resource-efficient pathway to evaluate quantum-enhanced fault diagnosis methods.

title: Verification Meets Calibration: Bounds and Secret-Independent State Preparation with an NV-Center as a Case Study
summary: Verification protocols provide cryptographic guarantees that the outcome of a delegated quantum computation is correct, a key requirement for scalable and trustworthy quantum computing. A central assumption underlying these protocols is secret independence: the noise affecting state preparation must not depend on the classical secrets that specify the prepared states. In earlier protocols this assumption was enforced by the physical separation of client and server; in the recent on-chip setting it becomes a property of the hardware itself, and one that high-fidelity devices do not automatically satisfy. We first make the requirement quantitative, deriving a bound that shows how residual secret dependence limits the size of any verifiable computation within this framework. Motivated by this, we introduce a calibration framework that enforces secret independence through pulse-level quantum control, producing state preparations that are simultaneously high-fidelity and secret-independent. We assess its performance on a nitrogen-vacancy centre system via emulation, showing that it reduces the secret dependence of the preparations by more than an order of magnitude compared to standard optimal control, and that it is robust against detuning and drive-amplitude errors commonly encountered in experiment. The framework operates entirely at the calibration stage and is platform-agnostic, offering a practical pathway towards verifiable quantum computing at scale.

AI.tldr: The paper quantifies how residual secret dependence of state-preparation noise limits verifiable computation size, then proposes a pulse-level calibration framework that enforces secret independence while preserving high fidelity, validated via NV-centre emulation.
AI.motivation: Verification protocols for delegated quantum computation rely on the assumption of secret independence: noise in state preparation must not depend on the classical secrets determining the prepared states. Previously ensured by physical client-server separation, this assumption now becomes a hardware property in on-chip settings, and high-fidelity devices do not automatically satisfy it. The work is motivated by the need to make this requirement quantitative and to enforce it practically.
AI.method: The authors first make the secret-independence requirement quantitative, deriving a bound showing how residual secret dependence limits the size of any verifiable computation within the framework. They then introduce a calibration framework that enforces secret independence via pulse-level quantum control, yielding state preparations that are simultaneously high-fidelity and secret-independent. Performance is assessed on a nitrogen-vacancy centre system through emulation.
AI.result: The calibration framework reduces the secret dependence of the preparations by more than an order of magnitude compared to standard optimal control, and it is robust against detuning and drive-amplitude errors commonly encountered in experiment.
AI.conclusion: Because the framework operates entirely at the calibration stage and is platform-agnostic, it offers a practical pathway towards verifiable quantum computing at scale.

title: Phase-Flag Access and No-Go Constraints on Quotient-Space Real Quantum Mechanics
comment: This work is a follow-up to our previous study, arXiv:2607.05865
summary: Barrios Hita et al. [Phys. Rev. Lett. 136, 240202 (2026)] proposed a quotient-space formulation of quantum mechanics over the real numbers and concluded that complex numbers are only a convenience. A preceding analysis [arXiv:2607.05865] showed that, when the construction is empirically equivalent to complex quantum mechanics, its real flag is protected by a hidden complex structure $\hat{J}$ and its composition rule is the balanced tensor product over that structure. Here we ask what would follow from the stronger operational reading that the flag is an accessible real degree of freedom. The answer is a direct clash with overlap-determinability (OD), introduced in [arXiv:2601.14638], and with standard no-go theorems. A readable or coherently controllable flag fixes a representative of each ray, and hence supplies precisely the phase convention that OD identifies as the missing resource for universal superposition of unknown states. Once promoted to a generic phase-access primitive, this resource enables probabilistic cloning of a linearly dependent set, steering-based signaling, and logarithmic-query unstructured search. Thus the quotient construction has a sharp follow-up interpretation: as a protected gauge representation it is standard complex quantum mechanics in real notation; as an accessible real theory it leaves the quantum operational framework.

AI.tldr: Analyzing the quotient-space real formulation of quantum mechanics (Barrios Hita et al., PRL 136, 240202, 2026), this paper shows that if its "real flag" were operationally accessible, the theory would violate overlap-determinability and standard no-go theorems, enabling probabilistic cloning, signaling, and logarithmic-query search—so the flag must be a protected gauge, making the construct merely complex quantum mechanics in real notation.
AI.motivation: Barrios Hita et al. concluded complex numbers are merely convenient via a quotient-space real formulation. The author seeks to test the stronger operational reading that the construction's real flag is an accessible real degree of freedom, and to determine what physical consequences follow from that interpretation.
AI.method: The author reasons from the prior result (arXiv:2607.05865) that whenever the quotient construction is empirically equivalent to complex quantum mechanics, its real flag is protected by a hidden complex structure Ĵ and its composition is the balanced tensor product over Ĵ. He then adopts the alternative premise—a readable or coherently controllable flag—and derives consequences relative to overlap-determinability (OD, arXiv:2601.14638) and standard no-go theorems.
AI.result: An accessible flag fixes a representative of each ray, supplying exactly the phase convention that OD identifies as the missing resource for universal superposition of unknown states. Promoted to a generic phase-access primitive, this resource yields probabilistic cloning of a linearly dependent set, steering-based signaling, and logarithmic-query unstructured search—placing the theory in direct clash with OD and no-go theorems.
AI.conclusion: The quotient construction has a sharp dichotomy: as a protected gauge representation it is just standard complex quantum mechanics in real notation; as an accessible real theory it abandons the quantum operational framework. The flag cannot be an operational real degree of freedom without contradicting established quantum constraints.

title: Bandwidth-Tunable Quantum Light Source at 1.5 $μ$m
summary: Quantum light sources constitute a crucial physical resource for the construction of quantum networks. Despite remarkable recent progress, there remains a lack of systematic investigation into the bandwidth tunability of quantum light sources under fixed waveguide parameters. In this work, we demonstrate a broadband quantum light source in the 1.5 $μ$m band with tunable bandwidth by changing the temperature of a piece of periodically poled lithium niobate waveguide. In our demonstration, the bandwidth of the quantum light source is tuned from 78.3 nm to 96.2 nm with a temperature change of 1 $^\circ$C . Under different bandwidths, the generation rates of correlated photon pairs are greater than 6.3 MHz with coincidence-to-accidental ratios consistently being no less than 608. The energy-time entanglement properties are measured by using the Franson interference with two-photon interference visibilities larger than 99.06%. Our results provide an effective method for developing the quantum light sources with tunable bandwidth which has great potential for building the large-scale quantum networks.

AI.tldr: A broadband quantum light source in the 1.5 μm band achieves tunable bandwidth (78.3–96.2 nm) by adjusting the temperature of a periodically poled lithium niobate waveguide by 1 °C, while maintaining high pair generation rates (>6.3 MHz) and strong energy-time entanglement (Franson visibility >99.06%).
AI.motivation: Quantum light sources are essential for quantum networks, but the bandwidth tunability of such sources under fixed waveguide parameters has not been systematically investigated.
AI.method: Temperature tuning of a periodically poled lithium niobate (PPLN) waveguide in the 1.5 μm band to control the bandwidth of the generated quantum light; characterization via correlated photon-pair generation and Franson interference measurements of energy-time entanglement.
AI.result: Bandwidth tuned from 78.3 nm to 96.2 nm with a 1 °C temperature change; correlated photon-pair generation rates above 6.3 MHz; coincidence-to-accidental ratios no less than 608; two-photon interference visibilities exceeding 99.06%.
AI.conclusion: Temperature tuning of a PPLN waveguide provides an effective method for realizing quantum light sources with tunable bandwidth, offering strong potential for building large-scale quantum networks.

title: Quantum Speedups for Log-Concave Sampling from Local Structure
summary: For a convex function $f \colon \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$, the problem of sampling from a distribution proportional to $e^{-f(x)}$ is called log-concave sampling. In many practical scenarios, the function $f(x)$ turns out to admit a local decomposition $f(x) = \sum_{a=1}^R ψ_a(x_{S_a})$. In this paper, we consider log-concave sampling using local queries, i.e., evaluation and gradient queries to each clause $ψ_a(\cdot)$, which can be computationally much cheaper than the queries to $f(x)$ itself. We show that if each coordinate appears in only a small number of clauses, there is a quantum algorithm for strongly log-concave sampling using $\widetilde{O}(\sqrtκd)$ local queries, where $κ$ is the condition number. This improves the prior best classical result $\widetilde{O}(κd)$ due to Ascolani, Lavenant, and Zanella (Ann. Probab. 2026) and the quantum result $\widetilde{O}(\sqrtκ d^2)$ implied by Childs et al. (NeurIPS 2022). Our quantum sampler applies to a broad class of locally structured models from statistical computing and machine learning, with representative examples including Gaussian Markov random fields, finite-element latent Gaussian models, and sparse generalized linear models. These results demonstrate that local structure is not merely an implementation detail, but a quantum algorithmic resource for high-dimensional sampling.

AI.tldr: This paper gives a quantum algorithm for strongly log-concave sampling under local (clause-wise) query access, achieving $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{\kappa}d)$ local queries when each coordinate appears in few clauses, improving over the best classical $\widetilde{O}(\kappa d)$ and prior quantum $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{\kappa}d^2)$ bounds.
AI.motivation: Sampling from $e^{-f(x)}$ (log-concave sampling) is fundamental, and in practice $f$ often decomposes locally as $f(x)=\sum_a \psi_a(x_{S_a})$. Queries to individual clauses $\psi_a$ can be far cheaper than queries to the full $f$, so the goal is to exploit this local structure to reduce the number/cost of oracle queries needed for high-dimensional sampling.
AI.method: A quantum algorithm for strongly log-concave sampling that uses local queries—evaluation and gradient queries to each clause $\psi_a(\cdot)$ rather than to $f$ itself—under the assumption that each coordinate participates in only a small number of clauses.
AI.result: Query complexity of $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{\kappa}d)$ local queries, where $\kappa$ is the condition number. This improves the prior best classical result $\widetilde{O}(\kappa d)$ (Ascolani, Lavenant, Zanella, Ann. Probab. 2026) and the quantum result $\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{\kappa}d^2)$ implied by Childs et al. (NeurIPS 2022).
AI.conclusion: The sampler applies to a broad class of locally structured models in statistical computing and machine learning, including Gaussian Markov random fields, finite-element latent Gaussian models, and sparse generalized linear models. Local structure is thus not merely an implementation detail but a genuine quantum algorithmic resource for high-dimensional sampling.

title: Multiparameter sensing of axion dark matter with superconducting-qubit networks
summary: We propose a quantum sensor network for direct detection of quantum chromodynamics (QCD) axion dark matter using entangled superconducting qubits. In the presence of a static magnetic field, the oscillating axion field induces a coherent qubit rotation described by an encoding angle proportional to the axion-photon coupling and an unknown dark-matter phase. Treating the phase as an additional unknown parameter turns axion detection into a two-parameter quantum estimation problem. We formulate these signals in Cartesian coordinates, thereby avoiding the singularity that arises in the weak-signal regime and establishing a regular framework for multiparameter quantum estimation. Using this framework, we optimize the quantum sensor network and combine it with Bayesian inference to reconstruct the axion-photon coupling. The optimized protocol accurately recovers the KSVZ and DFSZ benchmark couplings over the mass range $m_a\in[0.1,10]~μ{\rm eV}$, generalizes to previously unseen masses, and remains robust against realistic superconducting-qubit decoherence and gate errors.

AI.tldr: A quantum sensor network of entangled superconducting qubits is proposed for direct detection of QCD axion dark matter, reformulating axion detection as a two-parameter quantum estimation problem in Cartesian coordinates and optimizing the network with Bayesian inference to recover benchmark couplings across 0.1–10 μeV while remaining robust to qubit decoherence and gate errors.
AI.motivation: QCD axion dark matter is a leading candidate for dark matter, motivating direct-detection schemes. Existing approaches face a singularity in the weak-signal regime when the unknown dark-matter phase is treated as a parameter, which complicates multiparameter quantum estimation.
AI.method: In a static magnetic field, the oscillating axion field induces a coherent qubit rotation with an encoding angle proportional to the axion-photon coupling and an unknown dark-matter phase. Treating the phase as an additional unknown turns detection into a two-parameter quantum estimation problem. Signals are formulated in Cartesian coordinates to avoid the weak-signal singularity and establish a regular multiparameter estimation framework. The quantum sensor network is then optimized and combined with Bayesian inference to reconstruct the axion-photon coupling.
AI.result: The optimized protocol accurately recovers the KSVZ and DFSZ benchmark couplings over the mass range m_a ∈ [0.1, 10] μeV, generalizes to previously unseen masses, and remains robust against realistic superconducting-qubit decoherence and gate errors.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Cartesian-coordinate, two-parameter estimation framework enables optimized entangled superconducting-qubit sensor networks to directly detect QCD axion dark matter, achieving accurate coupling reconstruction, mass generalization, and robustness to realistic noise.

title: A Protocol-Guided LLM Agent for Quantum Program Synthesis and Execution
summary: This study evaluates a protocol-guided large language model (LLM) agent workflow for quantum program synthesis and execution. A versioned YAML protocol specifies interface and quantum-semantic requirements while leaving circuit design to the model. The workflow combines Qiskit circuit generation, evaluator-guided repair, and quantum processing unit (QPU) deployment. A matched ablation evaluates four LLM endpoints using the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) for H$_2$, the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) for MaxCut, and Fashion-MNIST quantum-kernel classification. Across 240 trials, protocol guidance increased evaluator completion from 80.0\% to 99.2\%, reduced mean repairs from 2.56 to 0.75, and reduced mean agent time from 55.70 to 30.58~s. Provider-reported token use decreased for three of four endpoints. Completed VQE trials meeting chemical accuracy increased from 16/40 to 29/40, while valid QAOA approximation ratios remained comparable. Semantic review identified rank-one fidelity kernels, reinforcing the distinction between evaluator completion and semantic validity. A 210-run IBM QPU study evaluated the combined generation-and-selection pipelines and confirmed deployment feasibility. The results support protocol guidance as a software-reliability layer that must be complemented by quantum-semantic validation.

AI.tldr: A versioned YAML protocol guiding an LLM agent workflow improves quantum program synthesis reliability—raising evaluator completion from 80.0% to 99.2% and cutting mean repairs and agent time—though quantum-semantic validity still requires dedicated review.
AI.motivation: LLM-based quantum program synthesis is promising but unreliable: generated circuits often fail interface and quantum-semantic requirements, requiring costly repair and execution cycles. The paper asks whether a structured protocol can act as a software-reliability layer and how far such guidance can carry synthesis toward semantically valid, deployable quantum programs.
AI.method: A versioned YAML protocol specifies interface and quantum-semantic requirements while leaving circuit design to the model. The workflow integrates Qiskit circuit generation, evaluator-guided repair, and QPU deployment. A matched ablation compares four LLM endpoints across three tasks—VQE for H2, QAOA for MaxCut, and Fashion-MNIST quantum-kernel classification—over 240 trials, followed by a 210-run IBM QPU study of combined generation-and-selection pipelines.
AI.result: Protocol guidance raised evaluator completion from 80.0% to 99.2%, reduced mean repairs from 2.56 to 0.75, and cut mean agent time from 55.70 s to 30.58 s; provider-reported token use fell for three of four endpoints. VQE trials meeting chemical accuracy rose from 16/40 to 29/40, while valid QAOA approximation ratios stayed comparable. Semantic review exposed rank-one fidelity kernels, underscoring the gap between evaluator completion and semantic validity. The QPU study confirmed deployment feasibility.
AI.conclusion: Protocol guidance functions as an effective software-reliability layer for LLM-driven quantum program synthesis, improving completion, efficiency, and token economy, but it does not guarantee quantum-semantic correctness. Protocol-guided synthesis must therefore be complemented by explicit quantum-semantic validation before downstream use.

title: QEncodeBench: Can Large Language Models Encode Classical Problems into Verified Quantum Oracles?
summary: Grover search, amplitude amplification, and quantum counting all rely on the same reusable subroutine, a phase oracle, whose construction the algorithms literature takes as given: the classical predicate is assumed to be already encoded as a correct, resource-bounded circuit. We turn this assumption into a measured capability. QEncodeBench tasks large language models (LLMs) with encoding classical constraint problems as phase oracles and scores the generated circuits with an adversarially self-validated verifier that decides full solution-set equivalence up to a global phase, with ancillas restored and resource budgets enforced. Sampled basis-state tests, we show, systematically overestimate this ability.
