Measured this way, models separate sharply: code models without a reasoning mode solve essentially nothing, and enabling native reasoning on identical weights improves accuracy by an order of magnitude. The failures are overwhelmingly semantic rather than syntactic. Two architectures, a unit-verified constraint agent and a neuro-symbolic compilation pipeline, close most of the remaining gap by delegating correctness-critical composition to deterministic procedures. Ablations quantify the contribution of each component, and resource gating exposes an architecture-dependent trade-off between circuit width and depth. Finally, controlled difficulty escalation reveals architecture-specific responses to difficulty structure: different difficulty axes degrade different methods, while the neuro-symbolic pipeline passes every evaluated instance. Code and data are available at https://github.com/chexujun/QEncodeBench.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces QEncodeBench, a benchmark that measures whether LLMs can encode classical constraint problems as correct, resource-bounded phase oracles for Grover search, amplitude amplification, and quantum counting, using a self-validated verifier that checks full solution-set equivalence up to global phase.
AI.motivation: The algorithms literature treats the phase oracle as a given, assuming the classical predicate is already encoded as a correct, resource-bounded circuit. The paper challenges this assumption, turning "oracle construction is given" into a measured capability and asking whether LLMs can actually perform this encoding.
AI.method: QEncodeBench tasks LLMs with encoding classical constraint problems as phase oracles. Generated circuits are scored by an adversarially self-validated verifier that decides full solution-set equivalence up to a global phase, with ancillas restored and resource budgets enforced. The paper also proposes two architectures: a unit-verified constraint agent and a neuro-symbolic compilation pipeline that delegate correctness-critical composition to deterministic procedures. Sampled basis-state tests are compared against the verifier to expose overestimation.
AI.result: Sampled basis-state tests systematically overestimate encoding ability. Models separate sharply: code models without a reasoning mode solve essentially nothing, while enabling native reasoning on identical weights improves accuracy by an order of magnitude. Failures are overwhelmingly semantic rather than syntactic. The two proposed architectures close most of the remaining gap. Ablations quantify each component's contribution, and resource gating exposes an architecture-dependent trade-off between circuit width and depth. Difficulty escalation reveals architecture-specific responses: different difficulty axes degrade different methods, while the neuro-symbolic pipeline passes every evaluated instance.
AI.conclusion: Phase-oracle construction is a non-trivial, measurable capability that current LLMs largely lack, and sampled testing hides this. Reasoning-enabled models and architectures that delegate correctness-critical composition to deterministic procedures substantially improve performance, suggesting that symbolic verification and neuro-symbolic delegation are key to reliable quantum oracle encoding.

title: Divergence Geometry of Quantum Multi-Mpemba Effects
summary: Whether a quantum Mpemba effect occurs can depend on how distance from stationarity is measured. We show that agreement across normalized operator-convex Petz divergences is decided by a one-parameter $χ^2$ profile. Its sign fixes the common order, alternating sign margins guarantee repeated crossings, and finite dimension yields a polynomial positivity test. The same profile explains diagnostic-independent late-time order for a simple real slow mode and isolates coherence as the local source of diagnostic dependence. In a trapped-ion qutrit ideal model, the reported preparation gives diagnostic-selective crossings, while a nearby preparation is a floating-point candidate for two family-wide reversals. The framework turns diagnostic robustness into a tractable control problem.

AI.tldr: Whether a quantum Mpemba effect (QME) appears depends on the chosen distance measure from stationarity. Agreement across normalized operator-convex Petz divergences is governed by a one-parameter χ² profile: its sign fixes the common order, alternating sign margins guarantee repeated crossings, and finite dimension gives a polynomial positivity test. This profile also explains diagnostic-independent late-time order for a slow mode and identifies coherence as the local source of diagnostic dependence, demonstrated in a trapped-ion qutrit model.
AI.motivation: The QME—anomalous speedup of relaxation toward stationarity—has been reported ambiguously because its existence can hinge on the diagnostic used to measure distance from stationarity. The paper aims to remove this diagnostic ambiguity by characterizing when different distance measures agree or disagree, thereby turning diagnostic robustness into a tractable control problem.
AI.method: The authors analyze normalized operator-convex Petz divergences and reduce diagnostic agreement to a one-parameter χ² profile. They use the sign of this profile to determine the common ordering, alternating sign margins to establish conditions for repeated crossings, and a polynomial positivity test in finite dimension. The analysis is illustrated with a simple real slow mode and a trapped-ion qutrit ideal model, comparing a reported preparation with a nearby alternative.
AI.result: Agreement across normalized operator-convex Petz divergences is decided by the sign of the one-parameter χ² profile; alternating sign margins guarantee repeated crossings; finite dimension admits a polynomial positivity test. The same profile yields diagnostic-independent late-time order for a simple real slow mode and isolates coherence as the local source of diagnostic dependence. In the trapped-ion qutrit model, the reported preparation gives diagnostic-selective crossings, while a nearby preparation is a floating-point candidate for two family-wide reversals.
AI.conclusion: Diagnostic dependence of the quantum Mpemba effect is captured by a single χ² profile, enabling a unified positivity/crossing criterion across Petz divergences. This converts the robustness of QME observations into a tractable control problem, with coherence identified as the key local source of diagnostic sensitivity.

title: Dissipative phase transitions in quantum reservoir computing
summary: Enhanced performance of quantum reservoir computing has been associated with dynamical phase transitions, but whether this connection extends to dissipative systems and which relaxation mechanisms underlie it remain insufficiently understood. We systematically compare driven-dissipative Kerr reservoirs across first-order and continuous dissipative phase transitions and find enhanced memory and nonlinear processing near both phase boundaries. Although the closure of the Liouvillian gap marks the transitions in the thermodynamic limit, computational performance does not generally follow gap suppression. An exact post-training Liouvillian-mode decomposition quantitatively attributes the trained memory to intrinsic relaxation channels. It shows that the gap mode contributes only weakly, while finite-rate modes and their cross-contributions dominate the enhanced capacity. These results go beyond phenomenological correlations by directly linking memory capacity to the intrinsic Liouvillian relaxation spectrum. Moreover, these findings provide a physical basis for designing dissipative quantum reservoirs and testing memory-enhancement mechanisms in experimentally accessible Kerr platforms.

AI.tldr: The paper links quantum reservoir computing performance to the intrinsic Liouvillian relaxation spectrum rather than to Liouvillian gap suppression, showing that finite-rate relaxation modes dominate the enhanced memory near dissipative phase transitions.
AI.motivation: Enhanced performance of quantum reservoir computing has been associated with dynamical phase transitions, but whether this connection extends to dissipative systems and which relaxation mechanisms underlie it remain insufficiently understood.
AI.method: The authors systematically compare driven-dissipative Kerr reservoirs across first-order and continuous dissipative phase transitions, and apply an exact post-training Liouvillian-mode decomposition to quantitatively attribute the trained memory to intrinsic relaxation channels.
AI.result: Enhanced memory and nonlinear processing are observed near both phase boundaries. Although the closure of the Liouvillian gap marks the transitions in the thermodynamic limit, computational performance does not generally follow gap suppression. The decomposition shows the gap mode contributes only weakly, while finite-rate modes and their cross-contributions dominate the enhanced capacity.
AI.conclusion: These results go beyond phenomenological correlations by directly linking memory capacity to the intrinsic Liouvillian relaxation spectrum, providing a physical basis for designing dissipative quantum reservoirs and testing memory-enhancement mechanisms in experimentally accessible Kerr platforms.

title: Entanglement Dynamics in Katz-Weighted Graph States
summary:
We investigate the entanglement dynamics of quantum states defined on graphs with non-local Ising interactions governed by the Katz kernel of the underlying network. The interaction pattern is physically motivated by a gapped fermionic mediator propagating on the same graph, whose perturbative elimination yields an effective Katz-weighted Ising Hamiltonian. Using the Entanglement Distance, we derive an exact analytical expression for the entanglement generated from an initially separable state and apply it to representative deterministic graph families.
  We then characterize the dynamics in different propagation regimes. In the weak-Katz regime, the dynamics admits a systematic motif expansion with triangles entering at first order order and four-cycles, local degree structure, and overlappin triangles appearing at second order. In the strong-propagation regime, the interaction is instead dominated by the principal adjacency mode and by the localization properties of its eigenvector. For Erdős--Rényi graphs, the weak-propagation expansion can be averaged analytically, revealing a locally tree-like contribution in the sparse regime and saturation of the Entanglement Distance density in the dense regime.
  Our results connect entanglement dynamics with both the walk-based and spectral structure of complex networks.

AI.tldr: This paper derives exact analytical expressions for entanglement generated from separable states under Katz-kernel non-local Ising interactions on graphs, and characterizes the dynamics in weak- and strong-propagation regimes.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to connect entanglement dynamics to both the walk-based and spectral structure of complex networks, motivated by a gapped fermionic mediator whose perturbative elimination yields an effective Katz-weighted Ising Hamiltonian on the same graph.
AI.method: Using the Entanglement Distance, they obtain an exact analytical expression for entanglement generated from an initially separable state, apply it to deterministic graph families, and analyze two regimes: a weak-Katz regime with a systematic motif expansion (triangles at first order; four-cycles, local degree structure, overlapping triangles at second order) and a strong-propagation regime dominated by the principal adjacency mode and eigenvector localization.
AI.result: For Erdős–Rényi graphs, the weak-propagation expansion is averaged analytically, revealing a locally tree-like contribution in the sparse regime and saturation of the Entanglement Distance density in the dense regime.
AI.conclusion: The results link entanglement dynamics to the walk-based and spectral properties of complex networks, providing exact, graph-family-dependent characterizations across propagation regimes.

title: The effects of shot noise on the quantum computation of NMR spectra
summary: Recent advances in the field of quantum computing hardware motivate the search for applications which demonstrate so-called quantum advantage. One promising use case that has been identified is the simulation of quantum many-body systems. The computational resources required for performing such a simulation on a classical computer generally grow exponentially with the size of the system being modeled, which is ultimately due to the exponential growth of the Hilbert space in which the dynamics of such a system take place. While digital quantum computers natively evolve quantum states directly in such a Hilbert space, thus naively avoiding this problem, the result of such a computation is typically not obtained as a deterministic output. Rather, it requires projective measurements which are fundamentally affected by shot noise. Any desired expectation values must therefore be reconstructed from repeated measurements, making the number of those measurements a relevant computational resource, and thus an important consideration for any potential claims of quantum advantage. In this work, we study how this resource scales with system size (a scaling which itself depends on the desired accuracy of the final result), using the simulation of nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra as a test case. We study this scaling for both real-world molecules, as well as a class of model NMR Hamiltonians which allow for efficient large-scale simulations with one-dimensional, two-dimensional, and all-to-all interactions. We find that the required resources increase only weakly with molecular size, far below the exponential growth of the underlying Hilbert space. This result suggests that shot noise should not pose a fundamental barrier to achieving quantum advantage in the simulation of NMR systems, and perhaps for many-body systems more broadly.

AI.tldr: This work analyzes how the measurement (shot-noise) resource required to reconstruct expectation values scales with system size for quantum simulation of NMR spectra, using both real molecules and model Hamiltonians. It finds only weak, sub-exponential growth with molecular size, suggesting shot noise is not a fundamental barrier to quantum advantage.
AI.motivation: Quantum advantage is expected for simulating quantum many-body systems, since classical simulation costs grow exponentially with Hilbert space size. Digital quantum computers evolve states natively in that space, but outputs require projective measurements affected by shot noise, so expectation values must be reconstructed from repeated measurements. The number of measurements is therefore a key computational resource whose scaling with system size must be understood before any quantum advantage claim, motivating a systematic study of this scaling.
AI.method: Using NMR spectra simulation as a test case, the authors study how the shot-noise-limited measurement resource scales with system size, with scaling depending on the desired accuracy of the result. They examine both real-world molecules and a class of model NMR Hamiltonians that permit efficient large-scale simulations with one-dimensional, two-dimensional, and all-to-all interaction topologies.
AI.result: The required resources grow only weakly with molecular size, remaining far below the exponential growth of the underlying Hilbert space across the studied molecules and interaction regimes.
AI.conclusion: Shot noise should not pose a fundamental barrier to achieving quantum advantage in simulating NMR systems, and likely for many-body systems more broadly.

title: State-Selective Floquet Memory in Degenerate Manifolds
summary: In order to understand which initial states retain memory under periodic driving, it is necessary to depart from the ideal limit giving rise to invariant structures and work inside near-degenerate manifolds. We show that degeneracy itself is not conclusive and what actually matters is how perturbations, such as structural and driving imperfections, acts on the projected multiplet. For systems decoupling into the local clusters in the ideal limit, the projections can be computed within degenerate perturbation theory. There the stability is decided by two criteria: the coupling can not connect the state with other degenerate partners in the manifold, either by kinetic blocking, or more generally, by diagonalizing the projected coupling, and the drive's local selection rule must admit only transfer energies detuned from Floquet sidebands, in which case the projected drive generator exactly vanishes. We formalize these understandings in a periodically driven clean, short-ranged alternating XXZ chain and demonstrate a set of results that include, long-lived states, both of product form and entangled across the clusters, a periodic family of sideband resonances, and an explicit example showing opposite fates for states with identical energy and charges.

AI.tldr: Memory retention under periodic driving is governed not by degeneracy per se but by how perturbations act on the projected multiplet; stability requires kinetic blocking or diagonalizable projected coupling plus drive selection rules detuning transfer energies from Floquet sidebands.
AI.motivation: To understand which initial states retain memory under periodic driving, one must depart from the ideal limit that produces invariant structures and instead work inside near-degenerate manifolds. Degeneracy alone is insufficient to explain memory retention, so the role of perturbations (structural and driving imperfections) on the projected multiplet needs clarification.
AI.method: For systems decoupling into local clusters in the ideal limit, projected couplings are computed via degenerate perturbation theory. Two stability criteria are established: (1) the coupling must not connect a state with other degenerate partners in the manifold, achieved either by kinetic blocking or, more generally, by diagonalizing the projected coupling; (2) the drive's local selection rule must admit only transfer energies detuned from Floquet sidebands, in which case the projected drive generator exactly vanishes. These ideas are formalized in a periodically driven clean, short-ranged alternating XXZ chain.
AI.result: The framework yields long-lived states of both product form and entangled across clusters, a periodic family of sideband resonances, and an explicit example showing opposite fates for states with identical energy and charges.
AI.conclusion: Degeneracy is not conclusive for memory retention under periodic driving; what matters is how perturbations act on the projected multiplet. The two criteria—kinetic blocking/diagonalizable projected coupling and drive selection rules detuning transfer energies from Floquet sidebands—determine stability, as demonstrated in the alternating XXZ chain.

title: VQE Validation on the Mononuclear T1 (Blue-Copper) Site: A Stepping Stone to the Multi-Copper Laccase Cluster
summary: Validating variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) pipelines on realistic chemical systems is a critical stepping stone toward tackling classically intractable molecules. In this work, we report emulator-based validation of the VQE workflow proposed for the copper active site, executed on the LRZ Eviden Qaptiva emulator. A problem-tailored ADAPT-VQE with a full singles-doubles-triples (S+D+T) pool removes over 99% of the correlation error, reaching a stable plateau at 4.03 mEh relative to exact diagonalisation (148 selected operators). This establishes a >40x improvement over the hardware-efficient ansatz (HEA). Finally, we frame these emulator results as a robust baseline for upcoming physical quantum hardware runs on Euro-Q-Exa.

AI.tldr: This work presents emulator-based validation of a VQE workflow for the copper active site on the LRZ Eviden Qaptiva emulator. A problem-tailored ADAPT-VQE with an S+D+T pool removes >99% of the correlation error, reaching 4.03 mEh above exact diagonalisation with 148 selected operators, a >40x improvement over the hardware-efficient ansatz (HEA).
AI.motivation: Validating VQE pipelines on realistic chemical systems is a critical stepping stone toward tackling classically intractable molecules. Here, the copper active site serves as a realistic target, and the emulator study aims to establish a reliable baseline before physical quantum hardware runs on Euro-Q-Exa.
AI.method: A problem-tailored ADAPT-VQE employing a full singles-doubles-triples (S+D+T) operator pool was executed on the LRZ Eviden Qaptiva emulator for the copper active site.
AI.result: The ADAPT-VQE removed over 99% of the correlation error, reaching a stable plateau at 4.03 mEh relative to exact diagonalisation with 148 selected operators. This constitutes a >40x improvement over the hardware-efficient ansatz (HEA).
AI.conclusion: The emulator results provide a robust baseline for upcoming physical quantum hardware runs on Euro-Q-Exa.

title: Neutral atom quantum computing for materials science and quantum chemistry
summary: Neutral atom arrays have emerged as versatile platforms for performing both digital and analogue quantum computing and simulation, with demonstrations ranging from large-scale programmable Hamiltonians realising topological phases or weighted graph optimisation to error-corrected logical qubits with transverse gate operations. This paper provides a broad overview to the neutral atom platform, and the potential applications relevant to materials science and quantum chemistry.

AI.tldr: A broad overview of neutral atom arrays as a quantum computing and simulation platform, covering their demonstrated capabilities and potential applications in materials science and quantum chemistry.
AI.motivation: Neutral atom arrays have become versatile platforms for digital and analogue quantum computing and simulation, yet a consolidated overview of the platform and its relevance to materials science and quantum chemistry is needed.
AI.method: Review/overview article: surveys the neutral atom platform and its demonstrated use cases, including programmable Hamiltonians for topological phases, weighted graph optimisation, and error-corrected logical qubits with transverse gate operations.
AI.result: The abstract reports no new experimental results; it catalogues existing demonstrations spanning large-scale programmable Hamiltonians and error-corrected logical qubit operations.
AI.conclusion: Neutral atom arrays constitute a versatile quantum platform with promising applicability to materials science and quantum chemistry.

title: Noise-Robust Quantum State Characterization for Remote State Preparation with Deep Learning
summary: Quantum communication underpins secure information processing and scalable quantum networks. In particular, remote state preparation (RSP) enables efficient quantum state transfer, but accurately estimating target states under complex noise remains challenging. Here, we propose a Transformer-based Quantum State Characterizer (TQSC) model for noisy RSP experiments. Our model reconstructs experimentally prepared pure and mixed photonic polarization states from noisy measurements in complex scattering environments, while its attention patterns provide physically grounded insights into correlations among the measured observables. The method achieves a mean estimator-target fidelity exceeding 99.999% under complex scattering and dynamic Gaussian noise, while its robustness and generalization are further examined using Qiskit-simulated Bloch-ball states.Furthermore, in a practical MNIST image transmission task with held-out states, the decoded bit error rate is reduced from 50.34% to zero after TQSC post-processing. The TQSC model enables accurate tomographic characterization under dynamic noise and provides physically grounded post-hoc insights, holding promise for intelligent quantum information processing applications.

AI.tldr: A Transformer-based Quantum State Characterizer (TQSC) reconstructs pure and mixed photonic polarization states from noisy remote state preparation measurements, achieving >99.999% fidelity under complex scattering and dynamic Gaussian noise and reducing an MNIST transmission bit error rate from 50.34% to zero.
AI.motivation: Quantum communication and remote state preparation (RSP) enable efficient quantum state transfer, but accurately estimating target states under complex noise remains challenging. Existing characterization approaches struggle with dynamic noise conditions.
AI.method: A Transformer-based Quantum State Characterizer (TQSC) model is applied to noisy RSP experiments. It reconstructs experimentally prepared pure and mixed photonic polarization states from noisy measurements in complex scattering environments. The model's attention patterns are analyzed to extract physically grounded correlations among measured observables. Robustness and generalization are tested with Qiskit-simulated Bloch-ball states and a practical MNIST image transmission task with held-out states.

AI.conclusion: The TQSC model enables accurate tomographic characterization under dynamic noise and provides physically grounded post-hoc insights, showing promise for intelligent quantum information processing applications.

title: Coherent error threshold for quantum LDPC codes
summary: A key appeal of quantum low-density parity check (qLDPC) codes is their ability to suppress stochastic Pauli noise below nonzero thresholds. Coherent errors are fundamentally different: they produce superpositions of error patterns whose amplitudes can interfere even after syndrome measurement. Rigorous understanding of coherent errors remains limited. Here we show that general qLDPC codes admit a nonzero code capacity threshold against local coherent noise and more generally local channel noise. For any family of qLDPC codes with distance $d=Ω(\log n)$, we show that there is a constant noise strength below which the logical recovery error in diamond distance decays exponentially with the code distance. The result is established for optimal recovery as well as the minimum-weight decoder. The key technical ingredient is what we call a \emph{cluster resummation}: rather than bounding superposed error configurations one by one, we isolate a large connected error cluster in the channel expansion and exactly resum all errors disconnected from it before taking norms. Standard cluster counting then yields exponential suppression. This work resolves a longstanding challenge in fault tolerance theory, providing general robustness guarantees for qLDPC codes against coherent noise and laying a rigorous foundation for future studies of fault-tolerant quantum technologies.

AI.tldr: General qLDPC codes admit a nonzero code capacity threshold against local coherent (and general local channel) noise: for any family with distance d=Ω(log n), below a constant noise strength the optimal and minimum-weight decoders achieve logical recovery error in diamond distance decaying exponentially in d, via a "cluster resummation" technique.
AI.motivation: qLDPC codes are valued for suppressing stochastic Pauli noise below nonzero thresholds, but coherent errors are fundamentally different—they create superpositions of error patterns whose amplitudes interfere even after syndrome measurement. Rigorous understanding of coherent errors was limited, and existing fault-tolerance guarantees did not generally extend to them.
AI.method: The authors prove a nonzero code capacity threshold for general qLDPC codes under local coherent noise and, more generally, local channel noise. Their key technical tool is "cluster resummation": instead of bounding each superposed error configuration individually, they isolate a large connected error cluster in the channel expansion and exactly resum all errors disconnected from it before taking norms; standard cluster counting then gives exponential suppression.
AI.result: For any family of qLDPC codes with distance d=Ω(log n), there exists a constant noise strength below which the logical recovery error in diamond distance decays exponentially with the code distance. This holds for both optimal recovery and the minimum-weight decoder.
AI.conclusion: The work resolves a longstanding challenge in fault-tolerance theory by providing general robustness guarantees for qLDPC codes against coherent noise, laying a rigorous foundation for future studies of fault-tolerant quantum technologies.

title: Technical Report OFDM-Assisted Simultaneous Quantum and Classical THz Communications
summary: The feasibility of cost-effective simultaneous quantum and classical communication (SQCC) transmitting both the quantum key and classical information via a superimposed coherent state is investigated both in optical and Terahertz (THz) bands. Since the existing THz SQCC schemes assume single-carrier (SC) transmission over flat fading channels, we embark on investigating SQCC in realistic frequency-selective multipath THz fading channels. We then propose an orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) based SQCC system for time-invariant frequency-selective THz scenarios, supported by low-density parity-check coded (LDPC) multidimensional QKD reconciliation schemes. Our simulation results demonstrate that the OFDM-based SQCC scheme is capable of achieving a practical secret key rate (SKR) over a wide range of power sharing scenarios between the classical and quantum signals. By contrast its single-carrier counterpart requires the classical signal to be at least 100 times stronger than the quantum signal in THz SQCC.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates simultaneous quantum and classical communication (SQCC) using superimposed coherent states in optical and THz bands, and proposes an OFDM-based SQCC system for realistic frequency-selective multipath THz fading channels, supported by LDPC-coded multidimensional QKD reconciliation.
AI.motivation: Existing THz SQCC schemes assume single-carrier transmission over flat fading channels, which does not reflect realistic frequency-selective multipath THz fading environments. This limits the practicality and power-sharing flexibility of SQCC.
AI.method: The authors analyze SQCC feasibility in both optical and THz bands, then propose an OFDM-based SQCC system for time-invariant frequency-selective THz scenarios, combined with LDPC-coded multidimensional QKD reconciliation schemes.
AI.result: Simulation results show that the OFDM-based SQCC scheme achieves a practical secret key rate (SKR) across a wide range of power sharing scenarios between classical and quantum signals, whereas the single-carrier counterpart requires the classical signal to be at least 100 times stronger than the quantum signal.
AI.conclusion: The OFDM-based SQCC approach significantly relaxes the power-sharing constraint compared with single-carrier THz SQCC, enabling more flexible and practical simultaneous quantum and classical communication over frequency-selective multipath THz channels.

title: Scalable logical qubits
summary: Utility-scale quantum computing will require executing long, complex algorithms with end-to-end error rates far below what physical qubits can support directly. Error-corrected logical qubits are needed to achieve this goal. To make the progress on logical qubits measurable and comparable we introduce the definition of scalable logical qubits: logical qubits preserved for long computations by repeated quantum error correction, capable of fault-tolerant universal operations with low-latency real-time decoding and feedback, and replicable to the hundreds or thousands, as required by applications. We characterize these scalable logical qubits along four coupled dimensions: reliability, scale, capability, and performance, and discuss trade-offs among these dimensions.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "scalable logical qubits" as a measurable and comparable benchmark for progress toward utility-scale quantum computing, defining them along four coupled dimensions: reliability, scale, capability, and performance.
AI.motivation: Utility-scale quantum computing requires executing long, complex algorithms with end-to-end error rates far below what physical qubits can directly support. Error-corrected logical qubits are needed to reach this goal, yet there is a lack of measurable and comparable criteria to track progress on logical qubits.
AI.method: The authors propose a definition of scalable logical qubits, characterized by three requirements: logical qubits preserved for long computations via repeated quantum error correction, fault-tolerant universal operations with low-latency real-time decoding and feedback, and replicability to hundreds or thousands as required by applications. They then analyze these qubits along four coupled dimensions—reliability, scale, capability, and performance—and discuss trade-offs among them.
AI.result: A framework is established that defines scalable logical qubits and organizes their assessment across four interdependent dimensions, while highlighting the trade-offs between these dimensions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed definition and dimensional framework provide a measurable, comparable standard for evaluating progress on logical qubits, supporting the path toward utility-scale quantum computing.

title: FT-Weave: Real-Time Compilation Framework for Reconfigurable Fault-Tolerant Quantum Architectures
summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) is essential for large-scale quantum computation, but realizing useful application throughput requires coordinating resource preparation, assignment, routing, and logical execution under strict hardware and timing constraints. Many FTQC compilation approaches construct offline schedules using nominal or fixed magic-state factory throughput. Such schedules cannot respond to stochastic resource-preparation and teleportation outcomes, leading to execution stalls and hardware underutilization. In this work, we introduce FT-Weave, a stage-aware real-time FTQC compilation framework that jointly coordinates resource preparation, resource assignment, teleportation routing, and correction handling. By adapting to runtime resource availability and hardware constraints, FT-Weave allows preparation, communication, and logical execution to overlap. We instantiate FT-Weave on two representative neutral-atom, early FTQC architectures: transversal STAR and a T-state cultivation architecture. Under the evaluated hardware and latency model, FT-Weave achieves a speedup of up to 3X over a baseline compilation flow for simulations of the two-dimensional transverse-field Ising model. In the case study, we further find that maximizing exposed concurrency does not necessarily minimize execution time. Although fine-grained asynchronous execution can reduce local idle time, its smaller optimization windows and increased routing contention can outweigh these gains. Together, these results show that effective runtime coordination, rather then exposed parallelism alone, determines how efficiently FTQC resources translate into application throughput:FT-Weave provides a blueprint for solving this real-time orchestration problem across resource protocols and architectures.

AI.tldr: FT-Weave is a stage-aware real-time compilation framework for fault-tolerant quantum computing that jointly coordinates magic-state preparation, resource assignment, teleportation routing, and correction handling, achieving up to 3X speedup over a baseline flow on two neutral-atom early-FTQC architectures.
AI.motivation: Many FTQC compilation approaches build offline schedules assuming nominal or fixed magic-state factory throughput. Since resource-preparation and teleportation outcomes are stochastic, such static schedules cause execution stalls and hardware underutilization. There is a need for runtime-coordinated compilation that adapts to actual resource availability under strict hardware and timing constraints.
AI.method: FT-Weave is a stage-aware real-time FTQC compilation framework that jointly coordinates four stages: resource preparation, resource assignment, teleportation routing, and correction handling. By adapting to runtime resource availability and hardware constraints, it overlaps preparation, communication, and logical execution. It is instantiated on two representative neutral-atom early-FTQC architectures: transversal STAR and a T-state cultivation architecture.
AI.result: Under the evaluated hardware and latency model, FT-Weave achieves up to 3X speedup over a baseline compilation flow for simulations of the two-dimensional transverse-field Ising model. A case study reveals that maximizing exposed concurrency does not necessarily minimize execution time: fine-grained asynchronous execution reduces local idle time but its smaller optimization windows and increased routing contention can outweigh the gains.
AI.conclusion: Effective runtime coordination, rather than exposed parallelism alone, determines how efficiently FTQC resources translate into application throughput. FT-Weave provides a blueprint for solving this real-time orchestration problem across resource protocols and architectures.

title: Experimental demonstration of finite-size general security via discrete-modulated CVQKD with real time postprocessing
summary: Continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CVQKD) is compatible with telecommunication infrastructure, but implementing composable security with experimentally practical resources has remained challenging, particularly for discrete-modulated (DM) protocols. We report the first experimental demonstration of a DM CVQKD system that generates composable secret keys against general attacks with finite-size block lengths on the order of $\sim 10^{6}$ rounds via a quadrature phase shift keying (QPSK) system. Our implementation follows a variable-length, general security framework enabled by modern entropy accumulation techniques and conic optimization, whose experimental pipeline allows real-time operation on near-commercial hardware.

AI.tldr: First experimental demonstration of a discrete-modulated CVQKD system generating composable secret keys against general attacks at finite-size block lengths (~10^6 rounds) using QPSK, enabled by entropy accumulation and conic optimization on near-commercial hardware.
AI.motivation: Continuous-variable quantum key distribution is compatible with telecommunication infrastructure, yet achieving composable security with practical experimental resources has been challenging, especially for discrete-modulated (DM) protocols.
AI.method: A variable-length, general security framework combining modern entropy accumulation techniques and conic optimization, implemented via a quadrature phase shift keying (QPSK) system, with an experimental pipeline supporting real-time operation on near-commercial hardware.
AI.result: Composable secret keys against general attacks were generated with finite-size block lengths on the order of ~10^6 rounds.
AI.conclusion: This work provides the first experimental demonstration of a DM CVQKD system achieving composable security under general attacks with practical finite-size parameters.

title: Proof of Shor's conjecture on the accessible information of quantum dichotomies
summary: The accessible information of any given quantum ensemble quantifies the maximum amount of Shannon information that can be extracted from the ensemble by any quantum measurement. Almost three decades ago, Shor conjectured that the accessible information of any quantum dichotomy, that is, an ensemble of two states, is attained by a projective measurement. Recently, a proof of this conjecture restricted to the qubit case was published by Keil. Here, we conclusively settle this longstanding open problem. First, we show that Shor's conjecture follows, in arbitrary dimension, from a recent result by Fang, Fawzi and Fawzi, and we provide a self-contained, elementary proof. Second, for any given dichotomy and measurement, we provide the explicit construction of a projective measurement that outperforms such a measurement in extracting information from the given dichotomy. Third, while the computation of the accessible information is known to be non-convex in general, we frame the computation of the accessible information of dihotomies as a convex problem.

AI.tldr: Shor's conjecture is proven: for any quantum dichotomy (ensemble of two states), the accessible information is attained by a projective measurement in arbitrary dimension. The authors derive this from a result by Fang, Fawzi and Fawzi, give a self-contained elementary proof, construct a projective measurement that outperforms any given measurement, and cast the dichotomy accessible-information computation as a convex problem.
AI.motivation: Shor conjectured nearly three decades ago that the accessible information of any quantum dichotomy (an ensemble of two states) is attained by a projective measurement. The problem remained open in general: only qubit case was recently proven by Keil. The paper aims to conclusively settle this longstanding open problem in arbitrary dimension.
AI.method: First, show that Shor's conjecture follows in arbitrary dimension from a recent result by Fang, Fawzi and Fawzi, and provide a self-contained, elementary proof. Second, for any given dichotomy and measurement, explicitly construct a projective measurement that outperforms the given measurement in extracting information. Third, reformulate the computation of the accessible information of dichotomies as a convex problem, despite accessible information being non-convex in general.
AI.result: Shor's conjecture is confirmed to hold in arbitrary dimension: projective measurements attain the accessible information for any dichotomy. An explicit outperforming projective measurement is constructed for any given measurement, and the accessible-information computation for dichotomies is expressed as a convex problem.
AI.conclusion: The longstanding open problem posed by Shor is resolved: the accessible information of any quantum dichotomy is attained by a projective measurement in arbitrary dimension. The work provides an elementary proof, an explicit outperforming projective measurement construction, and a convex formulation for computing the accessible information of dichotomies.

title: Quantum Noise Limited Nonlinear Phase-Preserving Amplification of a Bosonic Mode
summary: Does quantum mechanics allow for deterministic amplification schemes that simultaneously behave uniformly for all angles of bosonic phase space (i.e. phase preserving) and are nonlinear in the underlying field operators? Would such a scheme have some utility to quantum information science? In this paper we answer both questions with a resounding yes. Such amplifiers exist, but their form is highly constrained compared to the more general set of noise limited nonlinear amplifiers previously studied in the literature. This enables us to characterize the entire class of bosonic noise-limited nonlinear phase preserving amplifiers, and identify their utility: namely, the optimal amplification of Yurke-Stoler cat states and Kerr kitten states.

AI.tldr: The paper affirmatively answers whether quantum mechanics permits noise-limited nonlinear amplifiers that are phase-preserving and uniform across all angles of bosonic phase space, fully characterizing this restricted class and identifying its use for optimally amplifying Yurke-Stoler cat states and Kerr kitten states.
AI.motivation: Prior literature studied general noise-limited nonlinear amplifiers, but it remained unclear whether deterministic amplification schemes can simultaneously be phase-preserving (uniform for all bosonic phase-space angles) and nonlinear in field operators, and whether such schemes offer utility to quantum information science.
AI.method: The authors determine whether phase-preserving nonlinear amplifiers exist and show their form is highly constrained relative to more general noise-limited nonlinear amplifiers, then use this constraint to characterize the entire class of bosonic noise-limited nonlinear phase-preserving amplifiers.
AI.result: Phase-preserving nonlinear amplifiers do exist but are highly constrained compared with general noise-limited nonlinear amplifiers; the full class of bosonic noise-limited nonlinear phase-preserving amplifiers is characterized, and its utility is identified as the optimal amplification of Yurke-Stoler cat states and Kerr kitten states.
AI.conclusion: Quantum mechanics does allow deterministic, phase-preserving, nonlinear amplification schemes, and despite their constrained form they have concrete value for quantum information science, specifically for optimally amplifying cat-like and kitten-like nonclassical states.

title: Hardness of Pathfinding in a Welded Tree
summary:
Starting from the entrance of a welded tree, a quantum walk algorithm can find its exit vertex exponentially faster than any classical algorithm. However, it has been an open question whether any quantum algorithm is able to efficiently find a path from the entrance to the exit. We answer this by proving an exponential quantum query lower bound for finding such path. Specifically, for trees of height $n$, any quantum query algorithm requires at least $Ω(2^{n/24})$ queries in order to succeed with constant probability.
  Our proof uses the compressed permutation oracle technique in order to construct databases which track the graph information an algorithm has learned and forgotten, and show that no efficient quantum algorithm can build an entrance-to-exit path in these records.

AI.tldr: This paper proves an exponential quantum query lower bound for finding an entrance-to-exit path in a welded tree, showing that any quantum query algorithm requires Ω(2^{n/24}) queries for trees of height n to succeed with constant probability.
AI.motivation: While quantum walk algorithms can find the exit of a welded tree exponentially faster than any classical algorithm, it remained an open question whether any quantum algorithm can efficiently find a path from the entrance to the exit. This paper addresses that open question.
AI.method: The proof employs the compressed permutation oracle technique to construct databases tracking the graph information an algorithm has learned and forgotten, demonstrating that no efficient quantum algorithm can build an entrance-to-exit path in these records.
AI.result: Any quantum query algorithm requires at least Ω(2^{n/24}) queries to find an entrance-to-exit path in a welded tree of height n, succeeding only with constant probability. This establishes an exponential quantum query lower bound.
AI.conclusion: Finding a path from the entrance to the exit in a welded tree is exponentially hard for quantum algorithms, in contrast to the exponentially fast exit-finding result. This resolves the previously open question.

title: Multinegativity and single-letter formulas for asymptotic entanglement
summary: The study of entanglement inevitably leads to the concept of regularization, where measures are evaluated on infinitely many copies of a state. Single-letter formulas try to make these asymptotic entanglement quantities accessible through a calculation on one copy of a state, but are rarely available. We introduce a decreasing hierarchy of computable upper bounds on the asymptotic relative entropy of entanglement with respect to positive-partial-transpose (PPT) states. The regularization of every fixed hierarchy level equals this asymptotic quantity. Additivity at any level therefore yields a single-letter formula, even when the usual one-copy relative entropy is nonadditive. We establish such additivity at the first nontrivial level for two broad multiparameter families, both containing all Werner states. The upper-bound construction also extends to sandwiched Renyi divergences. The hierarchy motivates $k$-multinegative states, a generalization of binegative states and the associated $k$-multinegativity, which gives explicit upper bounds on both the asymptotic relative entropy and exact PPT entanglement cost. We construct states which are $k$-multinegative at arbitrarily large depths $k$ that separate consecutive levels of the previously introduced entanglement-cost hierarchy, disproving its conjectured finite collapse. These results provide state-dependent single-letter formulas while identifying a limitation of universal finite-level characterizations.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a decreasing hierarchy of computable upper bounds on the asymptotic relative entropy of entanglement with respect to PPT states, where each fixed level's regularization equals the asymptotic quantity, yielding single-letter formulas via additivity. It establishes additivity at the first nontrivial level for two multiparameter families (including all Werner states), extends the construction to sandwiched Renyi divergences, motivates k-multinegative states with explicit upper bounds, and constructs states disproving the conjectured finite collapse of the entanglement-cost hierarchy.
AI.motivation: Asymptotic entanglement measures require regularization over infinitely many copies, and single-letter formulas are rarely available. The work aims to make these asymptotic quantities computable through a hierarchy of tractable upper bounds.
AI.method: A decreasing hierarchy of computable upper bounds on the asymptotic relative entropy of entanglement (w.r.t. PPT states) is constructed, with regularization at each fixed level equaling the asymptotic quantity. Additivity is proven at the first nontrivial level for two broad multiparameter families. The construction is extended to sandwiched Renyi divergences, and k-multinegative states / k-multinegativity are introduced.
AI.result: Additivity at the first nontrivial level holds for two multiparameter families containing all Werner states, giving single-letter formulas even when one-copy relative entropy is nonadditive. k-multinegative states yield explicit upper bounds on asymptotic relative entropy and exact PPT entanglement cost. States that are k-multinegative at arbitrarily large depths separate consecutive levels of the entanglement-cost hierarchy, disproving its conjectured finite collapse.
AI.conclusion: The results provide state-dependent single-letter formulas while revealing a fundamental limitation of universal finite-level characterizations of entanglement measures.

title: Proof of a positive coherent-error threshold for topological quantum codes
summary: Threshold analyses of quantum error-correcting codes are well established for stochastic error models, in which errors occur randomly with given probabilities. However, errors in actual devices can also be coherent, such as unwanted $Z$ rotations due to imperfect control, which are not captured by stochastic error models. For the surface code, numerical studies have indicated threshold behavior even under coherent errors, but a rigorous proof of threshold existence is lacking. Here we prove that a positive threshold for coherent $Z$-rotation errors exists for quantum low-density parity-check codes with a bounded number of logical qubits, including the surface code and other topological codes. Specifically, we show that the maximum-likelihood Pauli recovery suppresses the entanglement infidelity exponentially in the code distance up to a prefactor linear in the number of physical qubits whenever the rotation angles lie below a constant that is independent of the code size. The proof combines Fourier analysis to retain the interference among the amplitudes of coherent errors with the cluster expansion of abstract polymer models. Our results expand the theoretical foundation of quantum error correction and offer a statistical-mechanical description of quantum error correction beyond stochastic errors.

AI.tldr: This paper proves the existence of a positive threshold for coherent Z-rotation errors in quantum LDPC codes (including the surface code) with a bounded number of logical qubits, showing that maximum-likelihood Pauli recovery exponentially suppresses entanglement infidelity in the code distance below a constant rotation angle independent of code size.
AI.motivation: Threshold analyses of quantum error-correcting codes are well established for stochastic error models, but real devices also exhibit coherent errors (e.g., unwanted Z rotations from imperfect control) that stochastic models do not capture. For the surface code, numerical studies suggested threshold behavior under coherent errors, yet a rigorous proof of threshold existence was lacking.
AI.method: The proof combines Fourier analysis to retain the interference among the amplitudes of coherent errors with the cluster expansion of abstract polymer models.
AI.result: The authors prove that a positive threshold for coherent Z-rotation errors exists for quantum low-density parity-check codes with a bounded number of logical qubits, including the surface code and other topological codes. Specifically, maximum-likelihood Pauli recovery suppresses entanglement infidelity exponentially in the code distance up to a prefactor linear in the number of physical qubits, whenever rotation angles lie below a constant independent of code size.
AI.conclusion: The results expand the theoretical foundation of quantum error correction and offer a statistical-mechanical description of quantum error correction beyond stochastic errors.

title: Quantum Simulation of Dissipative Non-Markovian Coupled Classical Oscillators
summary: We present a quantum algorithm for simulating classical oscillator networks characterized by non-Markovian dissipation and time-varying material properties, extending recent speedups for undamped harmonic systems to viscoacoustic and viscoelastic media. We embed the history-dependent dynamics into a Markovian state space governed by a non-Hermitian operator by approximating memory kernels through a Prony series. We then use linear combination of Hamiltonian simulation to estimate the instantaneous kinetic and potential energy for a subset of oscillators at time $t$ within error $ε$ using a number of queries to the oscillator system that scales as $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(α_{\rm tot} t/ε)$, where $α_{\rm tot}$ is polynomial in the strength of the dissipation, spring constants, inverse masses, and sparsity of the connections in the network. We further show that this energy estimation task is in the worst-case classically hard (i.e., a corresponding decision problem is $\mathsf{BQP}$-complete), even in the presence of strong dissipation. For time-dependent materials, we show that changes in material properties appear as effective dissipation or growth in the energy representation. Additionally, we prove the infeasibility of exponential quantum advantages in locally coupled topologies through a novel form of Lieb-Robinson-like bounds that apply to differential equations. This allows our quantum algorithms to provide quartic speedups for locally coupled damped oscillator systems in three dimensions, raising the possibility of practical quantum speedups for realistically damped oscillator networks and approximated wave equations.

AI.tldr: A quantum algorithm simulates classical oscillator networks with non-Markovian dissipation and time-varying material properties, achieving query complexity Õ(α_tot t/ε), proving BQP-completeness of energy estimation, and establishing Lieb-Robinson-like bounds that limit but still allow quartic speedups for locally coupled 3D damped systems.
AI.motivation: Recent quantum speedups for undamped harmonic systems need extension to realistic media (viscoacoustic, viscoelastic) featuring non-Markovian dissipation and time-varying material properties, with a rigorous assessment of classical hardness and achievable quantum advantage.
AI.method: Memory kernels are approximated by a Prony series to embed the history-dependent dynamics into a Markovian state space governed by a non-Hermitian operator. Linear combination of Hamiltonian simulation is then applied to estimate instantaneous kinetic and potential energy for a subset of oscillators.
AI.result: Energy at time t is estimated within error ε using Õ(α_tot t/ε) queries, with α_tot polynomial in dissipation strength, spring constants, inverse masses, and network sparsity. The energy estimation decision problem is BQP-complete (classically hard) even under strong dissipation. Novel Lieb-Robinson-like bounds for differential equations show exponential quantum advantage is infeasible in locally coupled topologies, yet quartic speedups are obtained for locally coupled damped oscillator systems in three dimensions.
AI.conclusion: The framework extends quantum simulation speedups to realistically damped oscillator networks and approximated wave equations, and provides matching hardness results and locality-based limits, indicating practical quantum speedups are plausible for 3D locally coupled systems.

title: $k$-fold unbiased measurements and maximal incompatibility
summary: Mutually unbiased bases capture perfect complementarity between two quantum measurements. Extensions beyond pairwise unbiasedness have been proposed, but essentially no non-trivial higher-order constructions are known. We introduce $k$-fold unbiased measurements ($k$-UMs), extending the $k$-fold unbiased bases notion of [arXiv:1706.04446] from rank-one basis measurements to arbitrary-rank projective measurements, and show that this higher-rank setting supports a much richer theory. We develop the notions of algebraic and spectral $k$-UMs and prove that they coincide for rank-one measurements and triples of measurements (3-UMs). We establish strong no-go results for higher-order rank-one constructions and three-outcome 3-UMs, but obtain infinitely many higher-rank triples using Hadamard matrices and Clifford algebras. We then give these structures an exact operational interpretation in terms of measurement incompatibility. For 3-UMs with any number of outcomes, we determine their generalised incompatibility robustness exactly and construct an explicit joint measurement for their noisy versions at the compatibility threshold. Finally, we implement the symmetry reduction of the sum-of-squares hierarchy recently introduced in [New J. Phys. 28, 064509 (2026)] and give numerical evidence that the noise thresholds arising from the $k$-UM analysis may characterise the asymptotic behaviour of this hierarchy. In particular, with very high precision, we numerically show that our constructed four-outcome 3-UMs are among the most incompatible triples of four-outcome measurements.

AI.tldr: The paper generalizes k-fold unbiased bases to arbitrary-rank projective measurements (k-fold unbiased measurements, k-UMs), develops algebraic and spectral k-UM theory, proves no-go results for higher-order rank-one constructions but constructs infinitely many higher-rank triples via Hadamard matrices and Clifford algebras, and gives an exact operational interpretation in terms of measurement incompatibility.
AI.motivation: Mutually unbiased bases capture perfect complementarity between two quantum measurements. Extensions beyond pairwise unbiasedness have been proposed, but essentially no non-trivial higher-order constructions are known. The authors aim to fill this gap by moving beyond rank-one basis measurements to arbitrary-rank projective measurements.
AI.method: The authors introduce k-fold unbiased measurements (k-UMs), extending the k-fold unbiased bases notion from rank-one basis measurements to arbitrary-rank projective measurements. They define algebraic and spectral k-UMs, prove coincidence for rank-one measurements and triples, establish no-go results for higher-order rank-one constructions and three-outcome 3-UMs, construct infinitely many higher-rank triples using Hadamard matrices and Clifford algebras, derive exact generalized incompatibility robustness for 3-UMs, and implement the symmetry reduction of the sum-of-squares hierarchy for numerical analysis.
AI.result: The higher-rank setting supports a much richer theory. Algebraic and spectral k-UMs coincide for rank-one measurements and triples of measurements (3-UMs). Strong no-go results hold for higher-order rank-one constructions and three-outcome 3-UMs, while infinitely many higher-rank triples are obtained. For 3-UMs with any number of outcomes, the generalized incompatibility robustness is determined exactly and an explicit joint measurement at the compatibility threshold is constructed. Numerical evidence shows the noise thresholds from k-UM analysis may characterize the asymptotic behavior of the sum-of-squares hierarchy, and the constructed four-outcome 3-UMs are among the most incompatible triples with very high precision.
AI.conclusion: Higher-rank k-UMs provide a rich extension of mutual unbiasedness with exact operational meaning in measurement incompatibility. The constructed four-outcome 3-UMs appear to be among the most incompatible triples of four-outcome measurements, and k-UM noise thresholds may characterize the asymptotic behavior of the sum-of-squares hierarchy.

title: Blind Quantum Computation with a Small Quantum Server
summary: Blind quantum computation (BQC) allows low-resource clients to securely delegate computations to a quantum server, but server resource costs scale with the computation size, posing a bottleneck for implementations. By leveraging Pauli-based computation (PBC), we achieve BQC with a server whose size depends only on the non-Clifford gate count. Our protocol inherits fault tolerance and qubit virtualization from PBC and reveals that classical-client BQC is possible even in the absence of classical simulability. Finally, we present an entanglement-based dual protocol that performs a resource state computation with a dramatically reduced execution cost.

title: Efficient Non-Uniform Quantum Hermite Transform through Adaptive Sampling
summary: On the span of the first $N$ oscillator modes, Gauss--Hermite quadrature gives an exact change of basis between mode coefficients and $N$ weighted position space samples. We implement this transform with $O(N\operatorname{polylog}(N,1/\varepsilon))$ logical gates and polylogarithmic quantum width. The operator-error bound $\varepsilon$ holds on arbitrary superpositions and includes all auxiliary registers. The construction uses signed averages on adaptive windows to convert uniform-grid samples into weighted Hermite-root samples. Their varying widths control the amplification cost, giving the near-linear bound.

AI.tldr: Gauss–Hermite quadrature yields an exact basis change between the first N oscillator (Hermite) modes and N weighted position samples; the authors give a quantum circuit implementing it with O(N polylog(N,1/ε)) logical gates, polylogarithmic width, and an operator-norm error bound ε that holds on arbitrary superpositions and accounts for all auxiliary registers, achieved via signed averages over adaptive windows that map uniform-grid samples to weighted Hermite-root samples.
AI.motivation: The first N oscillator modes form a natural finite-dimensional subspace for quantum simulation and computation, but converting between the mode-coefficient (Fock/oscillator) representation and a position-space sample representation is needed to implement position-dependent operations and measurements. A gate-efficient, low-width transformation with rigorous error control on arbitrary states—including ancilla registers—was lacking.
AI.method: A quantum algorithm implementing the exact Gauss–Hermite quadrature change of basis. Gauss–Hermite quadrature exactly relates the first N oscillator modes to N weighted position-space samples at the Hermite roots. The circuit first prepares uniform-grid samples, then uses signed averaging on adaptive windows to transform them into weighted Hermite-root samples. The adaptive, varying window widths govern the amplification/dilation cost, enabling near-linear scaling. Error is bounded in operator norm ε over arbitrary superpositions and includes contributions from auxiliary registers.
AI.result: A unitary (up to ε) transform realized with O(N polylog(N,1/ε)) logical gates and only polylogarithmic quantum width, with an operator-error bound ε valid on arbitrary superpositions and accounting for all auxiliary registers.
AI.conclusion: Gauss–Hermite quadrature provides an efficient bridge between oscillator-mode coefficients and weighted position samples; the adaptive signed-averaging construction attains near-linear gate complexity and polylogarithmic width with rigorous operator-norm error control, making mode↔position basis changes practical for quantum simulation and algorithm design.

title: Mermin-Peres magic rectangles modulo odd primes
summary: The Mermin-Peres magic square provides a simple example of a system of linear equations over $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ which has no classical solutions but does have a finite-dimensional operator solution. For a long time, it was not known how to construct similar examples over $\mathbb{Z}/d\mathbb{Z}$ with $d$ odd. In this paper, we construct, for every integer $d\ge2$, a linear system over $\mathbb{Z}/d\mathbb{Z}$ that has a finite-dimensional operator solution but no classical solution. For an odd prime $p$, our operators act on two $p$-dimensional qudits and generate a finite $p$-group obtained by adjoining diagonal polynomial phase operators to the generalized Pauli group. Classical inconsistency follows from an elementary linearity argument comparing assignments on abelian subgroups.

title: Quantum Entropy Contraction and Factorization from Hypercontractivity
summary: We prove that hypercontractivity implies entropy contraction for a single quantum channel, without a detailed balance condition. For primitive quantum Markov semigroups that are KMS-symmetric with respect to a faithful invariant state \(σ\), we obtain the modified Log-Sobolev bound $α_1\geq \fracλ{(2+\log\|σ^{-1}\|_\infty)}$ where $λ$ is the spectral gap. This removes the assumption of \(L_p\)-regularity for the comparison through the log-Sobolev constant. As an application, we show that the hypercontractivity of an average of two conditional expectations implies the approximate tensorization of relative entropy.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that hypercontractivity implies entropy contraction for a single quantum channel without detailed balance, deriving a modified Log-Sobolev bound and applying it to relative entropy tensorization.
AI.motivation: Connecting hypercontractivity to entropy contraction typically requires detailed balance and L_p-regularity assumptions. This paper aims to remove these restrictive conditions for a single quantum channel and KMS-symmetric semigroups.
AI.method: The authors establish an implication from hypercontractivity to entropy contraction directly for a single quantum channel. For primitive KMS-symmetric quantum Markov semigroups with a faithful invariant state σ, they relate the modified Log-Sobolev constant α_1 to the spectral gap λ via α_1 ≥ λ/(2+log‖σ^{-1}‖_∞), avoiding L_p-regularity.
