title: Procrastinating einselection in non-Markovian quantum dynamics
summary: Among the processes governed by open-system and dissipative quantum dynamics, environment-induced superselection, or einselection, is particularly foundational, since it describes the formation of a preferred set of pointer states through environmental monitoring and ultimately the emergence of classicality. Especially in the context of Quantum Darwinism, einselection can be studied in terms of the motion of an observable towards its pointer value. To this end, we derive a quantum speed limit for observables for finite-dimensional systems governed by differentiable time-local open dynamics. We identify two mechanisms through which non-Markovianity can enhance observable speed: direct dissipative motion supported by population retention or revival, and indirect enhancement through restoration of the asymmetry available for coherent motion. For permanent einselection, this delays the emergence of the pointer basis due to accumulated negativity.

AI.tldr: The paper derives a quantum speed limit for observables under time-local open dynamics, identifying two routes by which non-Markovianity slows pointer-state formation in einselection.
AI.motivation: Einselection—environment-induced superselection—is foundational for the emergence of classicality and is central to Quantum Darwinism, where it is studied via an observable's motion toward its pointer value. A bound characterizing how fast an observable can move is therefore needed to understand the timescales of pointer-basis formation under realistic, non-Markovian open dynamics.
AI.method: A quantum speed limit is derived for observables in finite-dimensional systems governed by differentiable time-local open dynamics (i.e., time-local master equations). The analysis decomposes observable motion to isolate distinct contributions, distinguishing direct dissipative motion from coherent motion and tracking how non-Markovian effects (information backflow, negativity accumulation) enter the bound.
AI.result: Two mechanisms by which non-Markovianity enhances observable speed are identified: (1) direct dissipative motion supported by population retention or revival, and (2) indirect enhancement via restoration of the asymmetry available for coherent motion. In the regime of permanent einselection, the accumulated negativity delays the emergence of the pointer basis.
AI.conclusion: Non-Markovianity can accelerate observable dynamics through population retention/revival and restored coherent asymmetry, but in permanent einselection this same accumulated negativity postpones pointer-basis emergence, thereby modulating the onset of classicality.

title: Analytic leakage suppression with a single control field: fast two-qubit gates with tunable couplers
summary: Simple analytic pulse-shaping techniques are of great practical utility in quantum control, with prime examples being the DRAG method for suppressing leakage in superconducting microwave gates and the transitionless-driving approach to shortcuts-to-adiabaticity. Standard versions of these methods require two orthogonal control channels, with the second channel effectively breaking time-reversal symmetry. This appears to rule out their use in settings with only a single real-valued control field, such as the kind of baseband flux control that is common in many superconducting circuit architectures. We show here that a simple analytic pulse-shaping technique derived via a Magnus expansion is effective even with just a single baseband control channel. We demonstrate its efficacy by simulating a two-qubit gate between transmons realized with a tunable coupler and baseband flux pulses. Our corrections dramatically reduce non-adiabatic leakage caused by ramping the coupler: for realistic device parameters, leakage in a fast iSWAP gate is suppressed by up to three orders of magnitude. Our approach is general, goes beyond simply suppressing unwanted spectral weight at leakage transitions, and can be applied to a variety of platforms.

AI.tldr: A simple Magnus-expansion-derived analytic pulse-shaping method enables effective control with a single baseband channel, dramatically suppressing non-adiabatic leakage in fast transmon iSWAP gates.
AI.motivation: Standard analytic pulse-shaping techniques like DRAG and transitionless driving require two orthogonal control channels, the second breaking time-reversal symmetry. This seemingly precludes their use in architectures restricted to a single real-valued control field, such as baseband flux control common in superconducting circuits.
AI.method: The authors derive a simple analytic pulse-shaping technique via a Magnus expansion that works with only a single baseband control channel. They validate it by simulating a two-qubit gate between transmons implemented with a tunable coupler and baseband flux pulses, applying their corrections to reduce leakage.
AI.result: For realistic device parameters, the corrections dramatically reduce non-adiabatic leakage caused by ramping the coupler, suppressing leakage in a fast iSWAP gate by up to three orders of magnitude.
AI.conclusion: The approach is general, extends beyond merely suppressing unwanted spectral weight at leakage transitions, and is applicable to a variety of platforms.

title: All causally separable quantum processes are quantum circuits with classical control of causal order
comment: Upon completion of this work we became aware of arXiv:2609.18559, which proves the same result as ours
summary: The concept of causal (non)separability describes whether the causal order between parties that perform local quantum operations is well-defined or indefinite. Causal (non)separability in the general multipartite setting was introduced and studied in [Oreshkov and Giarmatzi, New J. Phys. 18, 093020 (2016); Wechs, Abbott, and Branciard, New J. Phys. 21, 013027 (2019)]. We resolve an open problem from these earlier works by showing -- using a novel "coherent teleportation technique" -- that a sufficient condition for causal separability identified in [Wechs, Abbott, and Branciard, New J. Phys. 21, 013027 (2019)] is also necessary, and thus provides a complete characterisation of multipartite causal separability. A consequence of this result is that all causally separable processes admit a realisation as generalised quantum circuits in which the order between the operations is classically controlled, known as "quantum circuits with classical control of causal order".

AI.tldr: This paper proves the necessity of a previously identified sufficient condition for multipartite causal separability, thereby giving a complete characterization, using a novel coherent teleportation technique.
AI.motivation: Causal (non)separability in the multipartite setting was introduced in earlier works, which found only a sufficient condition for causal separability. Whether this condition is also necessary remained an open problem, leaving the characterization of multipartite causal separability incomplete.
AI.method: The authors employ a novel "coherent teleportation technique" to show that the sufficient condition for causal separability identified in prior work (Wechs, Abbott, and Branciard, 2019) is also necessary.
AI.result: The condition is proven necessary, yielding a complete characterization of multipartite causal separability. Consequently, all causally separable processes can be realized as generalized quantum circuits with classical control of causal order.
AI.conclusion: The open problem from earlier works is resolved: causal separability in the multipartite setting now has a complete characterization, and every causally separable process admits a realization as a quantum circuit with classical control of causal order.

title: Asymptotically Good Quantum Locally Testable Codes
summary: We construct explicit families of asymptotically good quantum locally testable codes over qubits. More precseily, we construct explicit quantum LDPC CSS codes over qubits having constant rate, constant relative distance and constant weight local testers with constant soundness.

AI.tldr: This work constructs explicit families of asymptotically good quantum locally testable codes (qLTCs) over qubits, achieving constant rate, constant relative distance, constant-weight local testers, and constant soundness via explicit quantum LDPC CSS codes.
AI.motivation: Prior to this work, it was open whether explicit asymptotically good quantum locally testable codes over qubits could exist—i.e., qLTCs simultaneously attaining constant rate, constant relative distance, and constant soundness. This paper addresses that gap by providing explicit constructions.
AI.method: The paper constructs explicit families of quantum LDPC CSS codes over qubits. The construction yields codes equipped with local testers of constant weight and constant soundness, while maintaining constant rate and constant relative distance.
AI.result: The authors obtain explicit asymptotically good quantum locally testable codes over qubits, with constant rate, constant relative distance, and constant-weight local testers possessing constant soundness.
AI.conclusion: Explicit asymptotically good quantum locally testable codes over qubits are achievable, resolving the question of their existence and establishing quantum LDPC CSS codes as a viable route to qLTCs with optimal parameters.

title: Parallel quantum channel discrimination and numerical ranges in tensor product subspaces
summary: Quantum channel discrimination plays a crucial role in quantum information theory. Of particular interest is the case in which the channels can be discriminated perfectly. In this work, we focus on the perfect quantum channel discrimination task in a parallel scheme. We develop an SDP formulation combined with a bisection procedure to compute a quantum state for perfect discrimination in time linear in the number of copies. In addition, we obtain the minimal number of copies of quantum channels to achieve perfect discrimination. Thanks to that, we settle in the affirmative Conjecture 1 of Duan, Guo, Li and Li [arXiv:1605.02294, IEEE ISIT 2016], which characterizes the number of parallel uses needed to discriminate perfectly a distinguished family of operator subspaces. All our results are obtained using the notion and basic properties of the numerical range. In particular, the key fact that we prove and use is that the minimal angle of the numerical range of a tensor product of matrix subspaces equals the sum of the minimal angles of the numerical ranges of the individual subspaces.

AI.tldr: This paper studies perfect quantum channel discrimination in a parallel scheme, provides an SDP-plus-bisection algorithm to construct a discriminating state in time linear in the number of copies, determines the minimal number of copies required, and affirmatively resolves Conjecture 1 of Duan, Guo, Li and Li, using numerical range techniques.
AI.motivation: Perfect discrimination of quantum channels is a key problem in quantum information theory. A previously open conjecture (Duan, Guo, Li and Li) characterized the number of parallel uses needed to perfectly discriminate a distinguished family of operator subspaces, but it lacked a proof and a general computational method for finding the discriminating state or the minimal copy number.
AI.method: The authors formulate the problem as a semidefinite program (SDP) combined with a bisection procedure, which yields a quantum state achieving perfect discrimination with complexity linear in the number of copies. They also derive the minimal number of channel copies needed. The analysis relies on the notion and basic properties of the numerical range, with the central technical result being that the minimal angle of the numerical range of a tensor product of matrix subspaces equals the sum of the minimal angles of the numerical ranges of the individual subspaces.
AI.result: An SDP-based algorithm with bisection computes a perfect-discrimination state in time linear in the number of copies; the minimal number of copies for perfect discrimination is determined; and Conjecture 1 of Duan, Guo, Li and Li is settled in the affirmative. The key supporting fact established is the additivity of the minimal angle of numerical ranges under tensor products of matrix subspaces.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides an efficient computational framework for perfect parallel quantum channel discrimination and resolves an open conjecture, demonstrating the utility of numerical range methods—especially the additivity of minimal angles under tensor products—for this class of problems.

title: Locally optimized variational evolution for quantum many-body systems
summary: Conventional quantum advantage in many-body dynamics is based on avoiding the simulation cost on a classical computer that arises from the extensive exponential complexity of the global wavefunction. Local observables, however, do not inherit this extensive complexity and may instead be governed by an intrinsic local complexity that is independent of the total system size. This distinction is particularly relevant in thermalising systems, where local observables lose memory of microscopic details and relax towards equilibrium values determined by only a few parameters. Here we introduce a variational time-evolution principle that exploits this distinction by replacing global-state fidelity with a cost function defined on local reduced density matrices. The resulting evolution retains coherent short-time dynamics while exploiting the simplification produced by thermalisation at later times. The concrete algorithm we propose is based on locally optimising matrix-product states and admits closed-form equations of motion analogous to the time-dependent variational principle. We show that the same variational principle has a quantum-classical counterpart, combining quantum evaluation of the local cost with an optimisation strategy robust to both shot and hardware noise. Proof-of-principle implementations on Quantinuum H2 and IBM Heron processors recover the characteristic local dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses the diminishing quantum advantage in simulating many-body dynamics when only local observables are of interest, since local observables are governed by size-independent local complexity rather than extensive global complexity. It introduces a variational time-evolution principle using a local cost function based on reduced density matrices, yielding a matrix-product-state algorithm with closed-form equations of motion and a noise-robust quantum-classical counterpart, validated on Quantinuum H2 and IBM Heron processors.
AI.motivation: Conventional quantum advantage in many-body dynamics stems from the extensive exponential complexity of the global wavefunction, which is intractable classically. However, local observables do not inherit this extensive complexity; they may be governed by an intrinsic local complexity independent of total system size. This distinction is especially pronounced in thermalising systems, where local observables forget microscopic details and relax to equilibrium values fixed by few parameters. The authors aim to exploit this distinction to design more efficient simulation schemes.
AI.method: The authors introduce a variational time-evolution principle that replaces global-state fidelity with a cost function defined on local reduced density matrices. The concrete algorithm is based on locally optimising matrix-product states and admits closed-form equations of motion analogous to the time-dependent variational principle. The same variational principle has a quantum-classical counterpart, combining quantum evaluation of the local cost with an optimisation strategy robust to both shot noise and hardware noise.
AI.result: The resulting evolution retains coherent short-time dynamics while exploiting the simplification produced by thermalisation at later times. Proof-of-principle implementations on Quantinuum H2 and IBM Heron processors recover the characteristic local dynamics.
AI.conclusion: By replacing global-state fidelity with a local cost function on reduced density matrices, the proposed variational principle efficiently captures local observables in many-body dynamics, leveraging thermalisation-induced simplification. The matrix-product-state algorithm and its noise-robust quantum-classical counterpart demonstrate practical viability, as confirmed by implementations on Quantinuum H2 and IBM Heron processors.

title: Environment Alignment and Redundant Record Formation in Imperfect-CNOT Quantum Darwinism
comment: 20 pages including references, 9 figures; plus 10 pages of Supplemental Material with 7 figures
summary: Quantum Darwinism explains objective information through redundant environmental records. Earlier work established that imperfect records can be amplified and that environment self-evolution can enhance or suppress their formation. We investigate how preparation, interaction angle, and field disorder combine in an imperfect-CNOT model with random Gaussian couplings and pure, noninteracting environment qubits. We find that, without fields, a single alignment parameter $Λ$ determines the preparation and interaction-angle dependence of conditional-state distinguishability. Increasing interaction imperfection or local field strength can improve or suppress recording. We explain this nonmonotonic response through the geometry of conditional branch separation. For the pure initial environments considered here, the $Z$ basis remains optimal for Holevo information, so field-assisted recording requires no change of the recorded system observable. Comparing uniform local field strengths with Gaussian-distributed strengths at equal root-mean-square strength shows how disorder broadens both beneficial and detrimental field effects. Exact expressions for fragment information and numerical simulations with up to 24 environment qubits quantify the distinction between high mean information and reliable records across fragments and throughout a finite observation window. These results connect the geometry of local information acquisition to the fragment sizes needed for robust recording. The branch-distinguishability analysis itself requires only the conditional evolution of each environment qubit and extends to other interactions that preserve a system pointer basis.

This paper aims to unify preparation, interaction angle, and field disorder within a controlled imperfect-CNOT model, and to connect the geometry of local information acquisition to the fragment sizes required for reliable recording.
